Just as this year, we were able to work through those, and I think as we get closer, we'll get a better sense for how the industry is responding.

James Schneider: Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Thanks, Jim.

Operator: Our next question today comes from Stacy Rasgon with Bernstein Research. Please go ahead.

Stacy Rasgon: Hi, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. For the first one, I understand that this more than $200 billion WFE next year is a constrained number. Do you guys have a point of view on what that number would be if it was not constrained, if clean rooms were available, if supply chain was not as tight as it is? I guess what I am asking is, what do you think the demand for WFEs in 2027 versus the supply number that you have given?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Listen, Stacy, you always ask these interesting questions. You know what I am going to ask. I love the question nonetheless. Listen, things are going to continue to be constrained, we think, in the next year by the things that we have described. I am not going to put a number on what the unconstrained demand would be. It would be higher. I am not going to give you a precise number. Like I said, we will fine tune what we think the number is and give you a little more specificity on the next quarter call also.

Stacy Rasgon: Okay, that is helpful. For my follow-up, any thoughts on the NAND upgrades relative to the services? It sounded like upgrades were strong. I do not know if that meant that they grew sequence or not. I assume they did because the NAND revenues grew a bunch, but the CSBG revenues were kind of flattish. I thought the upgrades were in CSBG. If that is the case, I guess what I am asking is, did upgrades drive the NAND growth? If they did, what else was going on in CSBG to absorb the growth such that the overall was flat?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Listen, Stacy, upgrades are a part of NAND and also CSBG. NAND also, when you go through these conversions, you need to buy new equipment also. Obviously, there was a contribution in demand spending from new equipment also.

Stacy Rasgon: Was it bigger than the upgrade piece? Sounds like it was.

Doug Bettinger: Both were meaningful contributors.

Stacy Rasgon: Okay. Thank you, guys.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Stacy.

Operator: Our next question today comes from Blayne Curtis at Jefferies. Please go ahead.

Blayne Curtis: Hey, guys. Thanks for squeezing me in. I actually want to ask on the NAND side, you mentioned SLC, that could be a big transition. Is that something you are seeing from customers, or is that still a potential transition?

Tim Archer: I think it is something that you are starting to hear from customers, talked about. Fundamentally, this idea of customizing memory and storage hierarchy to the different workloads, I think is now pretty well understood. I think that this is emerging as one of the potential solutions for low latency NAND access. I think if you go look just in the last recent days and weeks, there has been discussion of SLC+ NAND emerging as part of that stack. For a little bit longer time, there has been discussion also things like high bandwidth flash and the role it can play.

We are really starting to see NAND move from sort of a singular application we have always thought of, to now one in which perhaps the device performances themselves will need to be customized. That will have implications for us, but it will also from a process perspective. But really what we were highlighting here was the impact it would have on wafer capacity needs and therefore perhaps an uptick in NAND equipment demand.

Blayne Curtis: Thanks. I want to ask on advanced packaging, I think you said last time it would grow over 70% for the calendar year, I was curious what the update is. When you look at, it is probably at the smaller end, so you did not mention it, but in terms of that $200 billion outlook, any thoughts on advanced packaging growth next year?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Blayne, 70% for this year is still the right number. I would be stunned if advanced packaging didn't grow nicely next year.

Blayne Curtis: Yeah. Thanks, guys.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Blayne.

Operator: Our next question comes from Shane Brett at Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Shane Brett: Great. Thank you for letting me ask a question. My first question is on Foundry Logic. At your 2025 Analyst Day, you talked about your Foundry Logic SAM per wafer increasing 2x. Just how far are we towards that 2x with the shift from 3 nanometer, 2 nanometer, or if I rephrase that, how high did our SAM grow from 3 nanometer-2 nanometer? Do you think your share gains would accelerate with the transition to 1.4? Thank you.

Tim Archer: Yeah, that 2x was a multi-generational shift. It's a little bit hard to put exactly where we are in that. Maybe halfway through, if I thought about that roadmap that we gave there. But really, as we've moved forward though, we've seen just new emerging applications. I talked about a couple of them today. Clearly, advanced patterning itself is becoming ever more critical. We talked about the growth in Aether. We talked about the use of Akara for conductor etch. Backside power really starting to get a lot more attention, being a very etch and deposition intensive application. We just see a number of elements of that improvement. Then, I commented about how excited I was about advanced packaging.

Advanced packaging is playing a huge role within Foundry Logic and our exposure to the WFE there. I'm just saying Foundry Logic is turning into a good story. The thing we've highlighted over the last couple of calls, though, just to remind you, is the role we play in gate-all-around, our- Strength in ALD, in our strength in surface treatment. Those are areas where I think even at the Analyst Day, we might not have realized just how strong the uptake would be for things like the Argos surface treatment tool.

So I feel like the story just kind of keeps getting better and better the more complex the devices get across all three device types, foundry logic, DRAM, and NAND.

Shane Brett: Got it. For my follow-up, it will be on advanced packaging. SEMICON West, one of your colleagues had a great presentation on breaking the integration wall and advanced packaging for the AI era, with one of the highlights being key challenges to hybrid bonding adoption at scale. Just how does Lam enable hybrid bonding? Is more hybrid bonding better or worse for our advanced packaging share? Thank you.

Tim Archer: Well, I think that we participate in the elements of the process that help enable hybrid bonding. Obviously as a deposition and etch company, we do not do the bonding ourself, but we talked about a number of films, whether it is in the dielectric space or in the metal space, that ultimately play an important role in achieving successful hybrid bonding. There is an opportunity for Lam, through that transition. I think that overall, look the reality is success in advanced packaging, whatever version it is, will lead to greater adoption of advanced packaging, and ultimately, given our very high share position, that is a good thing for us.

Hybrid bonding or no, it is a very etch and deposition intensive process compared to other parts of the semiconductor manufacturing process itself. Thanks, Shane.

Shane Brett: Got it. Thank you very much.

Operator: Our next question today comes from Vijay Rakesh with Mizuho. Please go ahead.

Doug Bettinger: Vijay, are you there?

Operator: Vijay, your line is open, or are you perhaps on mute?

Vijay Rakesh: Oh, I was on mute. Sorry about that. Tim and Doug gave some interesting comments on the NAND side. You mentioned every 1% move to SLC requires about 2% increase in wafer capacity. As we look at next year with the move to SLC and potentially some HBF, any thoughts on how you think what percent of the market moves to SLC? Is it like 5% or how would you see that?

Tim Archer: I think it is too early for us to make any comment on that, and it would be probably something our customers should actually be commenting on. What you can rest assured is that in that sense, the intensity of Lam equipment in manufacturing those devices and those wafers would go up.

Vijay Rakesh: Got it. Then a quick follow-up. The advanced packaging side, you mentioned obviously there's a whole CoWoS and EMIB-T coming. I guess Lam has huge opportunities on the metallization pre-clean, TSV, et cetera. Just wondering if there's a way to size that opportunity, as you have done before for every 100,000 wafers of EMIB-T or CoWoS. How would you size that opportunity for Lam? Thanks.

Tim Archer: Yeah, I think maybe we'll take that as an action for some work to still be done. Maybe we're sizing that. We're not prepared to do that today.

Vijay Rakesh: Got it. Thank you. Thanks.

Doug Bettinger: Yep, you bet. Operator, we're going to take one more question.

Operator: Absolutely. Our final question today comes from Brian Chin at Stifel. Please go ahead.

Brian Chin: Hi there. Good afternoon. Thanks for letting us ask a few quick questions here. Maybe Doug, firstly, days of inventory kind of running a little bit over maybe a quarter at the moment. Clearly has drawn down. You said the turns have been really strong. Ideally, where would you want that to be?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, listen, we are super comfortable where it is right now. As the company scales up, you do get some level of efficiency offsetting that, though, right now we are trying to build inventory in anticipation of the growing demand we see into the next year. But I think we collectively feel pretty good about where we are at 3.4x.

Brian Chin: Okay, great. Maybe just the last question here. Is the $1 billion increase in your Aether revenue outlook reflective more of adding foundry logic and DRAM customers in terms of the adoption of that platform? Or is it more towards existing customers pulling forward introduction of the timing of Aether?

Doug Bettinger: I think it's a little bit of both. There have been some additional customer adoptions, but really it is as you really become POR for something like we mentioned, HBM manufacturing, and the volumes are growing there, the number of tools, and therefore the business just continues to expand. So we feel like we're positioned in production for some of the fast-growing parts of the market, and that's why we're able to take the number up.

Brian Chin: Great. Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Brian. Listen, thanks everybody for joining the call today. We're really excited about where the business is performing. We're really excited about what things look like into the next year, and I think we're probably the most excited about a third consecutive year of outperformance and an expectation that we're going to continue to drive those things into the next calendar year. So I know we'll see a lot of you guys in NDRs and conferences in the coming quarter, and we look forward to seeing you. Thanks for joining the call.

Operator: Thank you. That concludes today's conference call. We thank you all for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect your lines, and have a wonderful day.

news.Title: Meta (META) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Director of Investor Relations - Rob Bevegni

Chief Executive Officer - Mark Elliot Zuckerberg

Chief Financial Officer - Susan J. Li

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Good afternoon. My name is Krista, and I will be your conference operator. Today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to Meta's Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. All lines have been placed on mute to prevent any background noise. After the speakers' remarks, there will be a question-and-answer session. We ask that you limit yourself to 1 question. And this call will be recorded. Thank you very much. Rob, Bevagni, Meta's Director of Investor Relations, you may begin.

Mark Elliot Zuckerberg: Thank you. Good afternoon, and welcome to Meta Platform's third quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today to discuss our results are Mark Elliot Zuckerberg, CEO and Susan J. Li, CFO. Our remarks today will include forward-looking statements, which are based on assumptions as of today. Actual results may differ materially as a result of various factors, including those set forth in today's earnings press release and in our quarterly report on Form 10 Q filed with the SEC. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statement. During this call, we will present both GAAP and certain non GAAP financial measures. A reconciliation of GAAP to non GAAP measures is included in today's earnings press release.

Earnings press release and an accompanying investor presentation are available on our website at investor.@.com. And now, I would like to turn the call over to Mark. Alright. Hey, everyone. Thanks for joining today. This has been a busy and exciting few months. Our Family of Apps is now used by 3.64 billion people each day, and we are seeing all time highs in engagement on both Facebook and Instagram driven by strong growth in video. Threads has now overtaken x in monthly actives and to grow quickly. WhatsApp is hitting all time highs and is becoming an increasingly important platform for agents as well.

In the last few months, we have had several major milestones towards our goal of delivering personal superintelligence to everyone. We had 1 of our most successful launches ever with the Muse personal agent, We shipped Muse Wonder as our first frontier model. We shipped several new glasses and gadgets with Muse integration including coming soon to our new audio glasses.

We have been discussing our vision for personal superintelligence for more than a year, I want to help every person have an extremely capable personal agent that understands your goals and can help you achieve them and improve your life in whatever ways you want whether that is improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of. Muse is the product form of this vision. So now we have the foundational technology in place to deliver this. There is still a lot of work ahead, but our initial position is very strong.

Story Continues

In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up Muse personal agents, Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number 1 in the App Store almost every day. Engagement and retention are also off to a strong start, About 25% of people who have set up Muse use it on any given day. For our earliest adopters, the longer that they use Muse, the better the retention seems to get. So to put this in perspective, this is more than 2x the level that Threads started at or where we believe that other AI apps started at as well.

The most common use case for Muse is shopping. With more than 25% of people who are using Muse engaging in this with an average purchase size of over $200. Plaid told us that they had not seen activity like they are seeing with their connector on any other service before. And in the first week, we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected. Beyond shopping, the most common connectors are for personal productivity and connecting Muse to your other services like email and calendar.

Now this shows the importance of the Muse secure VM that we have built to provide state-of-the-art privacy and security we are looking forward to following up soon with the Muse confidential VM which will make it so that even Meta cannot see your content. We have also seen that Muse wonder improves quality engagement and retention further, which suggests that as we continue to improve intelligence, Muse will perform better and better over time. Now that Muse has clear product market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it. The goals for this next phase play to many of Meta's strengths.

We need to do 3 things, scale the product, grow revenue, and optimize compute costs. We expect to grow Muse to serve billions of people. This is both our mission and our strategy. it is our mission in that we believe in putting the power of personal superintelligence in everyone's hands. We believe that is the path to ensuring a positive future for everyone with individual empowerment as the source of prosperity, and balance of power is the foundation for safety. On a values level, we believe that delivering this capability widely is the best thing that we can be doing.

This is also our strategy because we think that billions of muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together. So we would like to create a large scale Muse network as quickly as possible. From a business perspective, the average revenue per American user for our existing Muse users is. Sorry. For our existing Family of Apps users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect that Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place. This will take some time, but we are starting to work on this now.

Our business model will have a few components. For most people, the product should be free, and we will build commerce tools so we get paid a fee based on the transactions that we help facilitate. We expect this will be paid for by businesses. For people who want the most advanced models or to use extra tokens, they subscribe directly and pay. For business owners who want additional features, to use Muse to grow their businesses or for companies that want people to use Muse for work, they will be able to subscribe directly and pay as well.

And for those who want Muse to help improve the personalization and quality of their content and ads across Meta, they will be able to connect to those experiences as well. Just to clarify, the average revenue that I was talking about before is the Family of Apps revenue for our existing Muse users. On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years. In the near term, Muse is very compute intensive to run. But we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.

If compute efficiency continues improving quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over the years. In the near term, the strength of our core business enables us to scale the Muse network before then, and we believe that we are the best positioned company to pursue this strategy. 1 other note on compute economics is that since training is a large fixed cost, now that we have leading models, we want to serve as much high margin inference demand as possible. That is why we are building the Meta Enterprise platform led by CJ Desai.

Muse, Wonder, and even more advanced models that we are training can serve additional high margin services beyond the Muse network including our API, Muse code, and other enterprise services. A fundamental feature of our business is that we have many good uses for this compute. It is difficult to forecast the exact growth rates for the Muse network, for our enterprise platform and for how Muse wonder and beyond will accelerate our core business. But through building up multiple ways to deploy these advanced models, we increase the chances that 1 or more of them significantly outperforms our expectations.

Beyond serving other businesses, we have not yet found the limit of how effectively we can apply compute to accelerating our own core business. We have implemented an evaluation with MuseWonder to improve how effectively it can autonomously improve our recommendation and ad systems. And as our upcoming models get even more advanced, I expect that we are going to see an increasing rate of improvement in these systems. Alright. Let's talk about the models now. MuseWonder is state-of-the-art across many dimensions that matter for personal superintelligence.

This validates the importance of training models ourselves to deliver the best experience, In addition to Muse, we have also seen that engagement per person in Meta AI has more than doubled since April, when we started rolling out our new models. While Muse Wonder has been our most important release, I have been very pleased with our pace of execution here. In the last few months, we have shipped Muse Spark 1.2 and 1.3, Muse code, 2 open weights models with Muse Glimmer and Muse Spark Open, also Muse Voice.

Going forward with the field advancing quickly, we plan to focus on both pushing the frontier of intelligence and distilling those models into much smaller and more efficient product models that will be optimized for personal agents. My view is that we will be able to build super intelligence through scaling, so we are methodically working our way up the ladder there. We are already working on larger models after MuseWonder, and they are going to be very impressive and capable. We are also working on new smaller models that are coming out soon that will deliver Muse Wonder intelligence more efficiently. Moving on, our work on personal superintelligence is now also the focus of Reality Labs.

Muse is coming to Meta Glasses starting next month, and that will be an important step towards this. People already love many features of the glasses already, music, calling, capturing moments, hearing assistance, and more. But over time, we expect Muse and having your personal super intelligence with you throughout the day will be the most important part of the experience. Muse is also central to the business model for the glasses. Again, our mission and strategy are to serve everyone here.

We believe in putting the power of this technology in everyone's hands So we have priced our devices not to make a large profit on the hardware, but to build a large software and superintelligence business on top of them over time. Glasses sales continue to grow rapidly, And now with Muse, we expect that paid subscriptions will increase and that this business will begin improving meaningfully from here. I also shared at Connect that we are changing our approach to virtual reality to only ship new devices when we have major breakthroughs like we had with the Meta VR glasses this year, which, of course, are the first VR experience ever in a pair of glasses.

I continue to believe that the path to delivering holographic experience of bringing together the physical and digital worlds and everyday glasses will come through VR first. But we will pace this aspect of our investment more to focus on delivering personal superintelligence first. So with these factors combined, we expect that the P&L of Reality Labs to improve from here with operating loss coming down to approximately $15 billion next year and trending towards profitability from there. Before we conclude, wanna spend a moment on the sheer velocity that we are seeing. An important part of our approach has always been to move fast. So we can learn quickly and serve people better at scale.

But recently, things have accelerated. The last year, we shipped edits, and it has already passed 50 million actives. New apps like Forum and Seller were built by small teams and are scaling quickly to serve power users. Muse went from an idea on a whiteboard to a successful product in just about 8 months, and we are about to ship Muse Charm, which will have gone from concept to a hardware device in people's pockets in less than 1 year. I am proud of what we are building. People have all kinds of different opinions about the future.

But at Meta, we believe that the future is for everyone and that putting power in people's hands is how we get there. I think that this matters, There needs to be a company out there that represents these ideas. But this is not just about ideas. it is also about execution. So I am grateful for everyone who is working so hard to deliver all of this to billions of people around the world, And as always, thank you to everyone who is on this journey with us. And now here's Susan.

Susan J. Li: Thanks, Mark, and good afternoon, everyone. Let's begin with our consolidated segment results. All comparisons are on a year over year basis unless otherwise noted. Q3 total Family of Apps revenue was $64.2 billion, up 26%. Q3 Family of Apps ad revenue was $63.1 billion, up 26% on both the reported and constant currency basis. In Q3, the total number of ad impressions served across our services increased 10%. Impression growth was healthy across all regions, driven by growth in engagement and users, as well as ad load optimizations. The global average price per ad increased 14% year over year driven by ad performance gains and improvements in macro conditions relative to Q3 of last year.

This was partially offset by strong impression growth particularly from lower monetizing surfaces and regions. Family of apps other revenue was $1.1 billion and grew 59%. Driven primarily by WhatsApp paid messaging and subscriptions revenue. Within our Reality Labs segment, Q3 revenue was $443 million, down 6% due to lower Quest headset sales, which were partially offset by continued strong growth in AI glasses revenue. Moving now to our consolidated results. Q3 total revenue was $64.6 billion. Up 26% on both a reported and constant currency basis. Total expenses were $51.6 billion, up 68% compared to last year, an included a $9.9 billion charge related to the August 2026 multistate attorneys general agreement.

Year over year growth was primarily driven by legal related costs infrastructure costs, and third party AI token costs. The growth in infrastructure costs was driven by higher third party cloud spend depreciation, and data center operating costs. We ended Q3 with over 66 thousand employees, down 12% from Q2 following the May 2026 headcount reduction. Third quarter GAAP operating income was $13 billion, representing a 37% decline year over year and a 20% operating margin. Excluding the Q3 legal charges related to the aforementioned legal settlement, our third quarter operating income would have increased 11% year over year. Our tax rate for the quarter was 24% above our outlook range primarily driven by the nondeductible portion of legal expenses.

Net income was $9.9 billion, or $3.83 per share. Capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, were $34.9 billion, driven by investments in servers, data centers, and network infrastructure. Free cash flow was negative $2.1 billion. We ended the quarter with $82.4 billion in cash and marketable securities and $83.7 billion in debt. Turning now to the business performance. There are 2 primary factors that drive our revenue performance our ability to deliver engaging experiences for our community and our effectiveness at monetizing that engagement over time. On the first, we continue to see significant gains from our content recommendation initiatives.

On Instagram, global time spent per user reached an all time high and grew double digits year over year in Q3 with strength across both reels and feed. On Facebook, Reels time spent reached all time highs both globally and in the US, with both growing double digits year over year. Threads also continued to scale with time spent per user growing over 20% year over year. Engagement gains across our services continue to be driven by improvements we are making to the relevance, personalization, and timeliness of the content we recommend. Investments into our recommendations engine across retrieval and ranking have continued to yield positive results on Instagram and Facebook.

For instance, on Instagram Reels, our relevance launches in Q3 increased Reels time spent by over 4%. Driven in part by our upgraded model architecture that ranks sequences of reels at a time instead of evaluating each reel independently. As well as improvements we made to add richer watch time watch-time signals. On Facebook Feed and Reels, we completed the global launch of a new generative retrieval architecture, which inspired by LLMs, labels pieces of content with semantic representations and generates potential recommendations. Helping our systems surface relevant new posts before they have accumulated significant engagement.

This new architecture is now rolled out to roughly 1-quarter of unconnected feed views and half of Reels views and increased Reels watch time by 1%. Our recommendations work is also helping us deliver fresher and more personalized content. Nearly 45% of recommended Reels are now less than 1 day old, up more than 11 percentage points from Q2. On Facebook reels, we doubled the amount of history our ranking model can consider. driving a 1% increase in Reels watch time in the US. LLMs are also helping us understand content more deeply. We continue to process public Instagram posts each day through LLM based content understanding systems.

These signals have improved the engagement with Instagram search results by 1% through the end of this quarter. This quarter, we also began moving our content understanding models onto our first party Muse model family. In offline evaluations, these models are outperforming our prior production models and are reducing per unit content processing costs by more than 80% across Instagram threads, Facebook, and ads. Beyond improving quality, owning more of this stack gives us greater flexibility to develop models around the signals that matter the most for personalization. Turning to the second driver of our revenue performance. Increasing monetization efficiency. We see significant opportunity to continue improving performance for the businesses who use our services.

Within our ad systems, we are continuing to drive performance gains as we deploy more predictive models that understand users more deeply and deliver ad experiences better aligned with their unique preferences while also making our infrastructure more efficient. Last quarter, we introduced Meta Generative Recommender, which uses LLMs to reason across ad content and user preferences to predict the best ad for each person. In Q3, we launched this approach to generative retrieval on Facebook feed, driving a nearly 2% increase conversions across targeted segments. In addition, we expanded our JEM model for ads ranking to additional surfaces, driving a 1.7% increase in conversions for off-site conversion campaigns and a 9.6% increase in app ad conversions.

And we continue to scale our retrieval systems efficiently. In Q3, improvements to Andromeda such as scaling model complexity and throughput, increased conversions by 1.4%. On Facebook. We are also leveraging AI to make it easier for businesses to manage campaigns develop creative, and act on performance opportunities. Meta AI Business Assistant is becoming a more proactive and capable partner for advertisers. We estimate that advertisers who adopted its recommendations drove almost 5% more conversions at the same cost per conversion and increased their advertising investment by 9% compared with similar non adopters. We are rolling out additional capabilities including creative insights, stronger business context, and more Agentic actions.

These features will allow marketers to plan, create, and optimize campaigns as well as schedule tasks and alerts through a conversational experience with approvals and previews that keep them in control. I will share 1 example of how Meta AI Business Assistant is empowering our advertisers. Simply Organic Maple, a family run maple syrup producer in Vermont, used Meta AI Business Assistant to improve its campaign messaging. After the Business Assistant recommended testing longer, more descriptive advertising copy, the business saw a 57% increase in purchases and a 36% reduction in cost per purchase. Its strongest revised ad delivered a 3x return on ad spend, a 52% improvement from the original.

Adoption of our generative AI ad creative tools also continues to scale. In Q3, nearly 10 million advertisers used at least 1 of these tools. Advertiser adoption of our video generation features grew 25% quarter over quarter, driven in part by ready made videos that reduce generation time to just a few seconds from a single image upload. Also expanding the opportunity at the intersection of creators and advertising. Partnership ads, which allow advertisers to run ads with creators, brands, and other businesses, continued to scale rapidly in Q3. Our partnership ads product grew over 97% year over year and surpassed $15 billion in annual revenue run rate.

In Q3, we also completed the global rollout creator marketing hub to all advertisers, bringing creator discovery, content and partnership ad activation into 1 place with more than 10 million creators now discoverable. We are integrating Meta AI Business Assistant into the hub so advertisers can conversationally search for creators, identify content to use in partnership ads, and get guidance across their creator marketing workflows. Outside of ads, we are also building out additional ways to monetize engagement across our ecosystem. In September, we announced the global expansion of Meta 1, our unified subscription service for consumers, creators, and businesses.

Meta 1 is rolling out gradually with more than 50 features across Facebook, and WhatsApp, including Meta Business Agent and Meta AI, and has surpassed 15 million subscriptions and trials to date. The core experience across our apps and Meta AI will remain free, while subscriptions offer more specialized capabilities and expanded AI usage. And beyond monetizing engagement across our existing services we are building new experiences and revenue streams around consumer agents. Mark highlighted the impressive early momentum with Muse. Users have found many reasons to use Muse with the top 3 categories being shopping, personal productivity, and creativity.

We are encouraged by the breadth of use cases with shopping in particular being used by over 25% of Muse weekly actives. While our near term priority is to grow adoption and expand Muse's reach, we see multiple paths to monetization beginning with subscriptions. We also see a significant opportunity to extend Muse to small businesses. Based on a recent user survey, we estimate that at least 500 million self identified small businesses use Meta's Family of Apps to reach customers and generate revenue. Muse could help these businesses acquire customers and operate more efficiently while helping people complete transactions. Over time, consumer and business agents could connect and transact directly creating opportunities around paid usage, commerce, and business services.

Alongside growth, we are focused on building sustainable unit economics. Muse's computing intensity means that expanding its user base will require significant investment, and we expect total serving costs to rise. At the same time, we expect to improve compute cost efficiency by more than 10x over the next year driven by better utilization of off peak capacity, more efficient models, and inference optimization. As revenue scales, these efficiency gains give us confidence in our ability to build a highly profitable business over time. Moving now to our financial outlook.

We expect fourth quarter 26 total revenue to be in the range of $73 billion to $76 billion Our guidance assumes foreign currency is an approximately 1% headwind to year over year total revenue growth based on current exchange rates. Turning to the expense and CapEx outlooks. Are raising our expense outlook to incorporate the $9.9 billion charge related to legal proceedings recognized in Q3. We now expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $175 to $179 billion. Excluding the Q3 legal charge, we continue to expect 2026 operating income to be above 2025 operating income.

At a segment level, we now expect Reality Labs losses to decline compared to 2025 to a range of $18 billion to $19 billion. For 2026, we anticipate capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion narrowed from our prior outlook of $130 billion to $145 billion. Absent any changes to our tax landscape, we expect our fourth quarter 26 tax rate to be between 15% and 17%. Additionally, we continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results.

For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States. Looking beyond 2026, we are still developing our budget and capacity plans for next year. But we expect to continue investing aggressively to support both our core business and emerging AI initiatives. Our current capacity and what is scheduled to come online gives us the flexibility to allocate resources across model training, core business growth, and the development and support of new products. Our AI investments are already delivering incremental advertising revenue through stronger engagement better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.

Building on this progress, our MSL investments are creating the foundation and infrastructure needed to unlock significant new revenue opportunities and strengthen capabilities across the business. While these investments will take longer to generate returns than those in our core business, the breadth of monetization opportunities and internal efficiencies gives us confidence in their long term potential. Looking ahead, although we are not providing a full year 2027 revenue outlook, The benefits our AI investments are delivering to the core business combined with emerging opportunities from model advances and product launches, position us to sustain strong overall revenue growth throughout 2027.

Separately, we remain focused on improving Reality Labs profitability As Mark mentioned, we expect losses to narrow next year to around $15 billion as we reallocate investment towards other priority areas. Primarily AI. Finally, today, we announced plans to create a new class of nonvoting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders. Through a stock dividend. For each existing share held, stockholders will receive 1 share of the new nonvoting stock. Effectively resulting in a 2-for-1 stock split. We expect trading to begin in late January 2027.

In closing, our business momentum continued in Q3 with strong execution across our core ads and engagement initiatives, And we are also excited by our progress towards bringing superintelligence to everyone. With that, Krista, let's open up the call for questions.

Operator: Thank you. We will now open the lines for a question-and-answer session. To ensure clarity. If you are streaming today's call, please mute your computer speakers. Your first question comes from the line of Brian Nowak with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Brian Nowak: Thanks for taking my questions. I have 2, 1 on Muse, 1 on Enterprise. Maybe at first, congrats on the success of Muse. But as you analyze the user behavior and the product, can you talk with us a little bit about any of the constraints to the slope of forward user growth that you are most focused on addressing, whether it is capabilities, model efficiency, capacity, etcetera, just so we understand what are the limiting factors to forward user growth that you wanna address. And the second 1 is on enterprise.

Mark, can you just sort of walk us through your vision, for the meta Enterprise product offering and the key value drivers you hope to provide for the enterprise adopting the service?

Mark Elliot Zuckerberg: Yeah. I think I can talk about both of those, and then Susan can jump in with anything else. Alright. So right now for Muse, we are 1 of the things I pointed out is we have more than 10 million people in the US and Canada who have set it up. But I think 1 of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute intensive service to run, we have not launched it globally yet. that is partially because of wanting to optimize it for each place, and there is some work around connectors for that. But it is it is partially that we wanna make sure that we do this efficiently.

So, I mean, there is pros and cons there. The pro, of course, is that just makes it even more impressive that you have 10 million people using it and signing up to use it in the first 6 weeks because those are all kind of Americans and Canadians in a small number of markets. So if we actually did roll it out more broadly, you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we are seeing today. But then on the flip side, we actually have to go do the work to bring the efficiency in line to make that make sense.

And so that. that is that is a big part of it that we need to do. We. The compute efficiency work is going to be important. On this also because you know, we wanna make sure that we have built enough compute to be able to serve what we think is going to be a billion plus people. If we can achieve certain compute efficiency targets, but we obviously have a lot of work to do there as well. And that will be that will be 1 of the limiting factors over the next year. We wanna build out the business around it. So, I mean, I talked about that.

And I think doing that in tandem with bringing down the compute or increasing the compute efficiency is going to be important for getting this to work from a business perspective. Which I am optimistic about. But I think that is 1 of the things that we need to do. And then there is just continuing to increase the value in the product. Which I think we will largely do by continuing to develop new models that is why I mentioned that you know, we launched Muse first on Muse Spark. And that is what is currently the default across the free tier. We rolled out Muse Wonder and people can access that in the in the paid tier today.

And we know that it performs a lot better, so we are working on getting a more efficient version of Muse. Wonder that we will be able to roll out more broadly, but you can imagine just as we iterate forward and, you know, 2, 3 models into the future when you have significantly higher intelligence and capability to solve many more problems for people and the ability to deliver that at a much more affordable price point, think that is going to just unlock a lot more value to people. So we are we are very excited about that.

Transitioning to talking about the enterprise piece, because I think of these 2 pieces, there is some connection here in that you know, the main enterprise offering in the near term is going to be the model API and Muse code, and we have business agents that we have been scaling for a while. And each of those 3 things is growing quite quickly. So we are excited about that. Over time, we would like to make it so that we have a whole kind of business network of Muse agents as well. there is the business agent, which we have talked about on previous earnings calls for businesses to help out with sales and customer support.

But what we see is a lot of activity. A lot of people are actually using Muse today to help run especially small businesses. And we think that there is both an opportunity to help create an agent that people use to really enable them to automate and do a lot of the parts of spinning up a small business that are just kind of difficult and time consuming, but are not the core thing that a person is trying to do. So we think that is a big deal. And then making a version of Muse that people can bring into different corporate environments and work there, we think is gonna be a big deal.

And then beyond that, building what I refer to as the Muse network, which is making it so that Muse is not just a kind of single player game. Where you have your Muse, but making it so that your Muses can work with your friends and your families. And if you wanna buy something, it is not just navigating to that business's website. it is talking to their agent. I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale. So I. I am I am very excited about all of that.

I think the enterprise use is gonna be a big part of it, but it is also going to kind of have this very valuable boost in the utility for consumers too. So I am I am very excited about both of those.

Susan J. Li: I would add on to Mark's comments on enterprise. AI is creating huge amounts of disruption in enterprise today. And, you know, we do not. What we can see, we really do not believe that traditional enterprise companies have this lockdown. And in fact, you know, some of the leading companies in this space today did not exist a few years ago. Those companies made large investments in model development and we have done the same. And we have increasingly competitive models to bring to bear for the benefit of all of our users, including small businesses and including enterprises, And already today, we have 500 million businesses, using our products.

So we really believe that AI is going to reshape how businesses operate. We expect that businesses of all sizes are going to use AI agents across software development and productivity, sales, marketing, and customer service, etcetera. We have differentiated assets to serve this market, bringing together models, infrastructure, global distribution, and long standing relationships with businesses. And it is our hope that this will be able to be a new diversified recurring revenue stream for us that will be able to support multiple business models, including subscriptions and usage based API and messaging and other revenue lines.

So we expect that this will be an opportunity that will develop over multiple years, and we intend to scale our investment behind demonstrated customer demand and product market fit in this area.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Eric Sheridan with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Eric Sheridan: Thanks so much for taking the questions. Maybe just the first 1 building on Brian's question. When you think about the friction points around Agentic commerce, how do you guys as a company think about solving for friction that is rising where there are aggregators or suppliers that do not want agents to interact with their platforms or their services, and how you think about lowering that friction or creating the right balance between the existing services that consumers access today relative to how this might all be changed or altered by Agentic behavior over the medium to long term.

And the second 1 would be with the announcement of the new class of shares tonight with earnings, any updated thoughts broadly about how you think about sources of capital and optimizing your capital structure to make sure you invest the proper amounts to capitalize on the opportunities that AI presenting in the next couple of years. Thanks so much.

Mark Elliot Zuckerberg: I can answer the first 1. So, okay. So the question-- what. sorry. What was the what was the first question there? Friction points around Agentic commerce. Got it. Alright. Yeah. So the right now, what we are seeing is that overwhelmingly, businesses are very excited about enabling this because they recognize that it is going to be a new opportunity for them not only to increase the sales and the quality of the experience for existing customers, but potentially to bring in new customers. So now, I mean, across the whole business ecosystem, different people will kind of adopt this at different paces.

And how our strategy evolves on that to develop the ecosystem will depend on how that goes. But overall, I would say we have been very positively surprised by how quickly I think a huge amount of businesses have wanted to know, not only figure out how to make it so that Muse can use their services more effectively, but have reached out to us to integrate around it. So I view that as a very good sign. And, you know, obviously, everyone wants to be an early adopter. that is fine. We will we will we will work with folks on the terms that makes sense for them.

But I do think that over time, this is gonna be quite valuable for everyone to make this work well, and I think we are on a good trajectory on that so far.

Susan J. Li: Yeah. I would add to that, and I will also answer your second question and just say, you know, I think agents are going to be an important part of you know, how reality evolves, and I think everyone is going to have to adapt to what that means, the new age of Agentic commerce. We obviously have had a lot of businesses who are very excited to partner with us. There are also businesses that are understandably focused on protecting customer relationships. And we expect the market, I think ultimately to evolve away from agents attempting to navigate every digital experience like a human.

And I think over the long run, this will move towards more permissioned structured interactions, and that will include authenticated APIs, approved agent partnerships, or direct communications between a consumer's personal agent and a business's own agent, and we are helping establish the standards needed to support that model. Earlier this month, we previewed the personal agent protocol and open standard across Muse and Meta business agents that we are developing with industry partners like Sierra, Walmart, Stripe, Shopify, etcetera. The protocols intended to define how a consumer's personal agent can interact securely and reliably with the business's agent and preserve appropriate controls for both the business and customer.

So, again, you know, I think adoption will likely be an even and will take time. And in the near term, we expect many experiences Will remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous. But, you know, as trusted integrations develop and agents demonstrate that they can generate incremental value and demand and operate safely, we expect that more and more businesses will be excited to participate. Your second question was about the announcement of the new class of shares.

So I should say, you know, we created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded nonvoting stock usable for, you know, capital raising employee compensation acquisitions, other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing class a and b shareholders. We believe this share class will maintain our founder led structure It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we are seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI. We do not have any specific financing plans to announce at this time.

But we thought it was prudent to establish the appropriate capital structure framework to ensure that we have access to a diverse pool of funding sources.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Douglas Anmuth with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Douglas Anmuth: Great. Thanks for taking the questions. I have 2. First, just wanted to follow-up on your last comment, Susan, just around as news evolves, and more businesses adopt agents, just wanted to get your sense of how things kind of and shift as you go to more permission based and agent to agent transactions? And, like, what does that really unlock over time And then, secondly, just on expenses and CapEx, thinking about 2027, I know you are not really there yet. But if I go back to some previous comments, you have talked about maximizing compute. In 2026 and 2027 and then having more flexibility in 2028.

A year ago, you talked about kind of notably larger dollar increase in 2026 than 2025, and then you have also used kind of growing operating income on an annual basis as well. So just curious if there is any of those that you can kind of apply or to help us think about 2027. Thanks.

Susan J. Li: Thanks, Douglas. So on your first question about how the Agentic ecosystem evolves, you know, I wish I could sort of, predict that more perfectly. And I think it will take some time. And, again, I think it will be a little uneven. But I definitely think that, you know, when I use Muse today, it is clear that there are a lot of parts of the experience that would be even better if Muse was able to interact more seamlessly with business agents on the other side.

For example, when you know, if Muse has to call a business on my behalf, I think it would be easier for the business if that call was handled by business agents that were representing it. And I think also 1 of the things that is really distinctive about Muse and 1 of the things that makes the product experience so great is the degree of proactivity that it exhibits on my behalf. Right? I can give it a task, and Muse is going to go execute against that task for me.

Even as I encounter some obstacles or, you know, cannot quite find the right thing and needs to chart a new path to helping me look for the thing I want.

And so I think the that sort of dimension of proactivity exhibited by either consumer agents or business agents, I think are going to enable more transactions to happen or more activity to happen broadly than happens today where, you know, when things are when more actions are taken primarily, you know, when, like, the latent demand expresses itself versus, you know, things where I can have Muse searching for things for me on an ongoing basis, giving me regular updates you know, on things I am looking for, sending me 10 new books a month, and agents should be doing similar things for businesses, and I think that creates sort of opportunities again for a new, more proactive sort of framework for what agent to agent interactions look like over time.

On your second question, which is about 2027, you know, we are quite early in developing our budget and capacity plans for next year. So you know, we are I would say, at the point where we are both investing sorry, evaluating a lot of investment proposals, you know, that have attractive return profiles over different time horizons, and we wanna figure out how we can fund as many of those as possible within, you know, the construct of our overall budget and financial goals.

But it is very dynamic, and it is still pretty early, and so we do not have anything more specific or quantitative to share until we get to the Q4 call, which is typically when we share guidance for the next year.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Justin Post with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Justin Post: Great. Thanks. 1 for Mark, 1 for Susan. Mark, you have got this powerful new model on your hands, and it seems like there is a lot you could do internally besides externally. But specifically to the ad business, you rearchitect your systems around AI. How much room is there for improvement as you deploy that new model? How are you thinking about that? And then for Susan, you mentioned strong revenue growth next year. Just wondering if that is advertising, or does that incorporate, some incremental AI revenues hitting next year? Thank you.

Susan J. Li: I am happy to take both of those. Go for it. Great. On your first question, you know, I think, our ads business has been benefiting for now many years from our ongoing investments in, you know, both kind of what we would have called traditional AI machine learning models and then, of course, from the sort of more recent generation of models. I would say that there are 3 themes there that I think are worth outlining. The first is just, you know, the kind of traditional road map of performance improvements. That we have in the pipeline based that is what I would describe more as business as usual machine learning work.

That continues to be a robust and healthy pipeline. And as we are looking into you know, into 2027, again, we are not providing an outlook, but I would say that our investments and product improvements across both engagement and ads initiatives give us, you know, confidence that we have meaningful runway to grow our core business throughout 2027, that also will gets to your second question also, but I should say, basically, I think the ranking and recommendations pipeline is healthy.

The second theme I would say is that, you know, we are excited about some of the new research bets that we have as we move into sort of a more LLM-oriented AI infrastructure to help us more deeply reason about people's preferences, what they are interested in both across organic content and recommendations, and we expect that we will be able to unlock we will be able to unlock benefits to our ranking and recommendations and from that research too.

And then the third thing is that we expect that generative AI tools, which have already been very valuable for advertisers, will continue to grow in terms of the features that we make available to advertisers primarily through the Advantage Plus suite. But features that make it easier for advertisers to quickly and seamlessly generate whether it is, you know, creative or take an image and generate video or generate sound, All, I think, in service of making the ads increasingly personalized for the person that they are being served to. So I would say we feel like there is, you know, meaningful runway across all 3 of those things. Your second question was about revenue growth next year.

And so as I mentioned, I think we are both, you know, feeling good about the budget investments that we expect we will make in both core ads and engagement initiatives next year. We are also, you know, building several new AI businesses, and we expect that those can begin contributing incremental revenue in 2027, but more importantly, can scale meaningfully over time, and those will include monetizing you know, our AI products through subscriptions, transactions, advertising, developing enterprise offerings as we talked about in 1 of the earlier questions.

So I would say while many of these opportunities remain early, and our near term focus is really on building high quality products, and achieving product market fit and scaled product market fit. I think our track record of reaching, you know, billions of people and building businesses at scale makes us feel good that AI is going to become a meaningful source of revenue diversification over time.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Mark Shmulik with Bernstein. Please go ahead.

Mark Shmulik: Yes. Thanks for taking my questions. Mark, coming out of Connect, you know, it kind of felt like we were ushering in the next era of the company, you know, in the business reorienting around kind of Muse at the center of everything. You know, is that a fair assessment of kind of how things are going internally? And, you know, and if so, can you just talk a little bit more about how some of the business mandates and outcomes may have changed? And then, Susan, you know, was interesting to kind of see the launch cadence where enterprise announcements kind of preceded some of the small business ones.

And, you know, I appreciate your comments on, you know, some of what is going on there around the SMB agent opportunity. But can you just share more details kind of the work required to serve and scale the offerings to SMBs? Thank you.

Mark Elliot Zuckerberg: Yeah. I mean, I can talk briefly about the first 1. I mean, look, It was more than a year ago that I think I wrote the letter about personal superintelligence as the North Star for the work that we are doing here. And it basically it fits with this line of work that we have done for more than 20 years at the company that is focused on empowering individuals, giving people a voice, giving people the tools to connect in the ways that they want, And when you extend that to the work around AI now, We think that the most important thing that we can be building for this next generation of techno.

Of technology is giving is basically putting the power of this technology in everyone's hands, which is the personal super intelligence vision. So we have been working on this for a while, and this is when we did the reboot around MSL and building the lab. A lot of it was this idea that we need to build models specifically to be good as personal agents. That we would be able to build the best experience by owning and building and designing ourselves the end to end technology So that includes the models and then the agents. And this has been this has kind of been in the works for a while.

I mean, the vision around the glasses has also been this. I mean, the we have wanted to build the next generation of hardware platforms that we can deliver the best end to end experiences to people. And think that is starting to come together as well, and I think will even more over the coming years. So, I mean, these are long term bets. I feel like this is what we are here to do is make long term technology bets and design the best experiences end to end that we can for billions of people around the world.

And I think as long as we continue to do that, then know, over time, the business takes care of itself as long as, you know, we continue executing well, which I am really proud of the team for how we are how we are doing on that. Thanks, Mark.

Susan J. Li: Your second question was around Muse for small business. So we launched we launched that, which you can think of as an expansion for Muse in late September and you know, rather than a separate product, it is kind of a new. A set of new skills and connectors inside the existing Muse app aimed at helping SMB owners, run operations, you know, find new customers. It connects to a business's, you know, for example, Instagram account analytics or Facebook pages or meta ad accounts. And if you click along with dozens of third party connectors that businesses already run on, like Shopify, QuickBooks, Canva, etcetera.

It already understands what businesses sell, brand voice, what customers are asking for, and muse can take actions including analyze ad and content performance, draft campaigns, responses, flag issues, you know, and we are actively listening to our SMB users to understand what their top use cases are. You know, we are seeing them use it for ads optimization, for direct message organizing, use it to expand their sales footprint, to keep their web current based on, you know, things like inventory and new products, to deal with employee load balancing.

So we are we are pretty closely following how business use Muse to make sure that we are being thoughtful about new features that we release in Muse to make it maximally useful and productive for SMBs. I would also say, you know, we have unique touch points to again, you know, I mentioned in my opening remarks, 500 million self identified small businesses. And, you know, we think that many of the investments that we make in consumer products are gonna carry over to help power those businesses also. We have, multiple excellent channels to surface those opportunities to small businesses globally.

So, you know, this is a place where we feel like we have an existing extremely strong platform, and we are very excited about it. And we also, you know, believe the transition to AI has broadly unlocked has broadly unlocked enterprises and new opportunity for us as well.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ross Sandler with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Ross Sandler: Great. Mark, you touched on this earlier, but could you elaborate a little bit on maybe some high level metrics around the per user cost structure of Muse today? Then how you see that cost curve coming down as you go forward. And what are some of the things you are doing? To bring that cost curve down? Thank you.

Susan J. Li: I am happy to answer that. And, Mark, you should add anything that you feel like I am missing. You know, we are not we do not have sort of specific numbers to share around the cost structure of Muse today, but, of course, it is, as Mark said, pretty compute expensive. And making sure that we are focused on compute efficiency is going to be 1 of the key vectors towards being able to both scale, use, and grow it into the business that we want. I think there are a couple dimensions of achieving that efficiency.

I think some of the more the more nearer term pieces, you know, include things like leveraging, you know, off peak or spare computing capacity, you know, to run some sets of jobs. Using smaller models. there is a lot of work to be done across different inference efficiency initiatives, all in service effectively of higher GPU utilization, and other product efficiency work we can do also.

And, you know, I think over the longer term, you know, I think this is a place where we expect that we are gonna be able to over time as LLMs scale get more tasks you know, done with fewer tokens and also rely on AI models themselves to help us improve the efficiency of the software that we use to run the model. So I think, it is a place where we both feel like there is a lot more, a lot more work on our efficiency road map that is going to help us, you know, bend the curve. Here.

And we also expect that the sort of arc of how the of how the sort of AI driven technological advances are going to apply here will also help us achieve larger savings over time.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Mark Stephen Mahaney with Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.

Mark Stephen Mahaney: Okay. Thanks. 2 questions. You know, there is a bit of a playbook or there has been an Meta over the years when you surface new surfaces. And, you know, you build up the user growth engagement, then you layer in monetization. Do you think it is sort of a similar playbook here? Or it has. Does it have to be a little bit faster with Muse just given that the costs associated with it are materially greater arguably than launching those surfaces in the past.

And then just a clarification on that commerce data point that you provided, about 25% of users and the $200 or greater ASP Are you including in commerce travel, up purchases or is that just a retail data point? Thank you.

Mark Elliot Zuckerberg: My guess is, I think that we are going to work on monetization somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook. For a couple of reasons. 1 is just the size of the numbers that we are talking about in terms of both the cost and the and the opportunity, I think, make it kind of important to make progress on that in order to be able to scale it. The other is just that such a large part of what people are doing is commerce. And to your question, that does include travel too.

I think we might view travel as a different case, but travel is actually 1 of the other top use cases for Muse is basically people planning that out and planning different kinds of things that they would get and they might get through our family of apps. So I think that this is this is going to be an important thing for us to work on to deliver the consumer value that people want And in doing so, I think we will be able to build a model where we get a percent of the value that we are helping to create for people.

So I know that is gonna be. it is gonna be very important to kind of get the math on all of this to work out. So that way we can continue the compute build out that we wanna build in order to get this to reach everyone at scale.

And in addition to everything that Susan said in response to the last answer, I would also just add that, like, we just see this trend that you know, year over year, you know, I just expect that we will be able to deliver the same intelligence that we have now in MuseWonder or frankly any of the current frontier models at a fraction of the cost in a smaller model a year from today. So to the extent that represents some kind of baseline level that people, you know, seem to you know.

That kind of is sufficient for product market fit for Muse, I think that we will just continue through kind of continued model development, make progress on that efficiency. The thing that is of course, less clear is that I do not think in a year from now, most people are going to wanna use the current model level of intelligence, because that is also gonna make progress. So think we are gonna need to work on all of these things, both the revenue pieces of it and scaling the different aspects of that as well as progressing on the model development.

All the efficiency in order to be able to know, both fund and support the compute build out and reach billions of people. Which, again, we wanna get to that. as soon as possible. Part of the reason why we are not, you know, just charging everyone up front to use this is we want to establish this Muse network, and we think that it is going to be more valuable for people at scale when there are a lot of people and businesses using Muse. So that way, they can collaborate and work together. I think that is really a very important state to get to. And 1 that we are quite excited about.

And, again, do not think that there are many companies in the world that are well situated to be able to do that in the way that we are. I think we are very well situated to do that, and we plan to push on that quite aggressively.

Operator: And that does conclude our question-and-answer session. Mr. Bevagni, I would like to turn the call back over to you. Thank you for joining us today, and we look forward to speaking with you again soon. Ladies and gentlemen, this does conclude today's conference call. Thank you for your participation and you may now disconnect.

news.Title: 統一證券：台股短線動能回溫，中期整理結構尚未完全扭轉
news.Content:
【昨日盤勢】：

受經濟部公布9月外銷訂單連四月改寫單月歷史新高的激勵，台股展現多頭反彈氣勢。盤面呈現「金融穩盤、電子點火」的良性架構。金融股大漲2.55%，扮演穩盤定海神針；電子族群則百花齊放，其中被動元件表現最為強勢，成為多頭衝鋒旗手；此外，矽晶圓、IC封測及太空衛星概念股同步走揚，顯示資金並未退場。權值股方面，台積電上漲0.62%、鴻海上漲3.51%、聯發科下跌0.24%、廣達上漲2.49%，台達電上漲1.24%。盤面強勢股，華新科、台表科、精材、GIS-KY、聯茂、玉晶光、信昌電、上品、台勝科等漲停；南亞、景碩、穩懋、高力、京元電子、欣銓、昇達科、晶豪科、宏致等漲幅6%以上。盤面弱勢股，聯一光、柏承跌停；智邦、德宏、泰合、巨虹等跌幅6%以上。終場台灣加權指數上漲594.84點，以46887.77點作收，成交量8331.91億元。三大類股全面上漲，電子上漲1.08%、傳產上漲1.74%、金融上漲2.55%。次族群方面，以玻璃陶瓷、電腦及週邊設備、資訊服務表現較佳，分別上漲2.17%、1.34及0.42%。次族群方面，以塑膠、光電、金融保險表現較佳，分別上漲6.52%、3.61%、2.55。

【資金動向】：

news.Title: Lam Research Q1 Earnings Call Highlights
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in Lam Research Corporation? Here are five stocks we like better.

Record September-quarter results: Lam Research reported $8.22 billion in revenue, up 22% sequentially and 54% year over year, with record 52.4% gross margin, 40.2% operating margin and $2.20 in non-GAAP EPS.

Strong AI- and memory-driven outlook: Lam forecast December-quarter revenue of $8.6 billion and expects 2027 wafer-fabrication equipment spending to exceed $200 billion, led by DRAM, leading-edge foundry logic and NAND demand.

Growth remains constrained by capacity and supply: Near-term component shortages and clean-room limitations could delay shipments, while China revenue is expected to decline significantly in the December quarter. Lam generated record $3.24 billion in free cash flow and returned approximately 41% of it through buybacks and dividends.

From High Dividend Growth to High Yield, These 3 Stocks Just Boosted Dividend Payouts

Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) reported record revenue, profitability and earnings per share for its September 2026 quarter, as demand tied to artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductor manufacturing and packaging continued to support spending on deposition and etch equipment.

Revenue for the September quarter totaled $8.22 billion, up 22% sequentially and 54% from the same period in 2025, Chief Financial Officer Doug Bettinger said. The company recorded a gross margin of 52.4%, an operating margin of 40.2% and diluted non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.20, all records. Operating margin exceeded 40% for the first time, according to the company.

→ The AI Sell-Off Continues—These 3 Stocks Keep Raising Guidance Anyway

Analysts Just Raised Price Targets On These 3 Semiconductor Equipment Stocks

"In the September quarter, Lam again delivered record revenue and profitability," President and Chief Executive Officer Tim Archer said. He said AI-driven semiconductor demand and rising device complexity were increasing the intensity of deposition and etch processes across memory, logic and advanced-packaging applications.

December Outlook and WFE Forecast

For the December 2026 quarter, Lam forecast revenue of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million. The company expects gross margin of 52.5%, plus or minus one percentage point; operating margin of 40.5%, plus or minus one percentage point; and earnings per share of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15.

→ Tesla's Roadster Reveal Hints at 2 Much Bigger Moves

Why Lam Research Still Looks Like a Buy After a 300% Rally

Bettinger said the December revenue outlook would have been "a little bit higher" without near-term supply-chain constraints. He did not quantify the impact, but said shipments delayed from the December period because of timing would move into the March quarter.

Story Continues

Lam expects calendar-year 2026 wafer-fabrication equipment, or WFE, spending to be in the mid-$150 billion range. Its preliminary forecast for 2027 calls for more than $200 billion in WFE spending, with percentage growth led by DRAM, followed by leading-edge foundry logic and NAND.

→ Luxury's Middle Market Is Cracking—These 3 Stocks Could Win

Archer said clean-room availability and supply constraints for certain components may limit the industry's ability to fully meet demand in 2027. The company is working with suppliers to expand capacity, he said, and expects to improve the supply situation shortly. Bettinger added that Lam expects 10 new Tier 1 fabs to come online during 2027.

At the midpoint of its December-quarter outlook, Lam expects calendar-year 2026 systems revenue to grow more than 40% year over year. Archer said the company expects 2026 to be its third consecutive year of WFE outperformance, supported by growth in Lam's served available market and product share gains.

Memory and Foundry Demand Drive Growth

Memory represented 46% of September-quarter systems revenue, unchanged from the prior quarter, while foundry accounted for 46%, up from 44%. Logic and other applications represented 8% of systems revenue.

Memory systems revenue reached a record dollar level and increased 120% from a year earlier. NAND accounted for 26% of systems revenue, compared with 23% in the June quarter, as customers continued converting to 256-layer and higher-class devices. NAND revenue rose about 40% sequentially, and Lam said it is seeing initial spending on 384-layer-class devices.

DRAM revenue also reached a record, with spending focused on technology additions and upgrades at the 1α, 1β and 1γ nodes for DDR5, LPDDR5 and high-bandwidth memory. Archer said Lam expects etch and deposition intensity to increase as DRAM architectures become more three-dimensional.

The company also discussed potential new NAND demand related to AI storage tiers. Archer said QLC NAND supports cost-effective data storage, TLC is used for higher-bandwidth context-memory and key-value-cache workloads, and SLC-class NAND is emerging for low-latency access in agentic AI applications.

Lam said shifting NAND production from TLC to SLC-class devices reduces bits per device by roughly three times. For every one-percentage-point shift of NAND bits toward SLC-class devices, about 2% more installed wafer capacity would be needed to support the same bit demand, according to the company.

Technology Investments and Advanced Packaging

Archer said foundry logic and DRAM accounted for about 80% of Lam's systems-revenue growth year to date. The company highlighted demand for its Akara etch, conductor etch and Aether dry-resist products in advanced patterning applications.

Lam said its Aether dry-resist solution has demonstrated sub-10-nanometer resolution with High-NA EUV and can reduce exposure dose by 10%. Aether products are ramping in high-volume HBM manufacturing using Low-NA EUV, Archer said. Lam now expects cumulative Aether-related revenue to reach about $2.5 billion by the end of the decade, approximately $1 billion above its previous expectation.

The company also cited opportunities in backside power delivery, where it has secured tool-of-record wins for four products at a leading customer. In advanced packaging, Lam said its Syndion etch product won four new positions across multiple customers for advanced logic and HBM through-silicon-via applications.

Lam expects advanced-packaging revenue to grow about 70% during calendar 2026. Archer said panel-level packaging is an emerging growth opportunity, with Lam having shipped panel plating systems to more than 20 customers globally. The company expects to achieve panel-level packaging market share exceeding its position in current wafer-level packaging.

Regional Mix, Services and Capital Returns

China represented 35% of September-quarter revenue, up from 26% in the June quarter, due to investments from domestic and multinational customers. Bettinger said China's contribution is expected to be significantly lower in the December quarter, primarily due to lower domestic-customer revenue, while multinational demand in the region should remain reasonably strong.

Korea accounted for 20% of revenue and Taiwan contributed 18%. Lam's Customer Support Business Group generated nearly $2.5 billion in revenue, its fourth consecutive quarterly record and a 40% increase from a year earlier. The company expects full-year 2026 CSBG revenue growth of more than 30%, followed by growth of more than 15% in 2027.

Lam generated record free cash flow of $3.24 billion in the September quarter. It repurchased about $1 billion of shares and paid $325 million in dividends, returning roughly 41% of quarterly free cash flow to shareholders. The company ended the quarter with $7.5 billion in cash and short-term investments and $3 billion remaining under its authorized share-repurchase program.

About Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX)

Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) is a semiconductor equipment company that develops and manufactures systems used to fabricate integrated circuits. Its technologies support key stages of wafer processing, helping semiconductor manufacturers create the increasingly complex structures found in memory, logic and other types of chips.

The company's product portfolio includes etch systems, which selectively remove materials from wafers; deposition systems, which apply thin films; and cleaning solutions used to remove contaminants and residue during manufacturing.
