news.Title: Cathie Wood Trimmed Ark's Alphabet Stake Even as Google Search Revenue Grew, While Ark Piled Into Rocket Lab Even After Its Neutron Launch Delay. Is Ark Betting Against the Wrong AI Winner?
news.Content:
On Sept. 22, Cathie Wood's Ark Invest bought roughly $25.1 million of Rocket Lab (NASDAQ: RKLB) shares, while selling $5.8 million of Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) stock. However, Rocket Lab has since encountered another setback in its growth plans. On Oct. 14 , the company announced that its Neutron rocket's first launch had been delayed until 2027. Despite this setback, Ark Invest purchased another $9.3 million of Rocket Lab shares on Oct. 15.

Ark's investment decisions highlight the trade-off between Alphabet's established profitability and Rocket Lab's potentially higher, but less certain, long-term growth.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Alphabet's AI investments are showing results

Alphabet's search advertising revenue growth was not driven solely by higher ad prices. The company's paid clicks rose 13% year over year, while average cost per click increased 3% year over year in the second quarter. Google Cloud revenue also jumped 82% year over year to $24.8 billion, and operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion in the second quarter. These numbers show stronger advertising monetization and profitable cloud growth, although Alphabet doesn't separately disclose AI profits.

Alphabet's upcoming third-quarter results on Oct. 28 could provide further clarity on its AI investments. J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth expects Google Cloud revenue to double year over year, partly driven by solid demand for Google's custom AI chips. However, Alphabet has also guided for $195 billion to $205 billion in capital expenditures for 2026. With such massive spending, sustaining revenue growth while protecting profit margins will be increasingly important.

Why Ark remains interested in Rocket Lab

Ark's investment thesis relies on a possible shortage of launch capacity in the U.S. in the coming years. The investment firm expects Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), better known as SpaceX, could retire its existing Falcon 9 rocket launch system by the end of 2030, while increasingly using its next-generation Starship rocket to support orbital AI data centers. This could create opportunities for competing launch providers, including Rocket Lab, as government agencies, communications providers, and other commercial customers seek alternatives to SpaceX.

Story Continues

Rocket Lab already has evidence of commercial demand. The company has entered a multiyear launch deal with Synspective for 20 launch missions using its operational Electron rockets. The company also exited the second quarter (ending June 30, 2026) with a backlog of $2.36 billion. Rocket Lab's space systems segment, which manufactures satellites, spacecraft components, and related equipment, accounted for nearly 81% of the second-quarter revenue. Hence, Rocket Lab's existing business is not entirely dependent on Neutron's success.

However, realizing Ark's expected launch-market opportunity depends on Neutron becoming commercially successful. Rocket Lab has secured a launch contract with Kepler Communications for satellites supporting on-orbit computing, but the mission is scheduled no earlier than 2028. Hence, even a successful first Neutron launch in 2027 cannot guarantee regular, profitable operations.

Rocket Lab has also raised $1.94 billion by issuing 29.3 million shares to help fund its planned acquisition of Iridium Communications . While the deal could add recurring revenue, the share issuance also dilutes existing shareholders.

Rocket Lab is currently trading at over 39 times trailing-12-month sales, leaving very little room for execution missteps. Alphabet is trading at just close to 9.3 times sales, despite established profitability and more visible AI monetization. Hence, Alphabet currently appears to offer the stronger risk-adjusted AI investment opportunity, although Rocket Lab could deliver greater returns if its ambitious expansion succeeds.

news.Title: Meta Platforms (META) Reports Q3 Earnings: What Key Metrics Have to Say

The reported revenue compares to the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $63.41 billion, representing a surprise of +1.88%. The company delivered an EPS surprise of +13.5%, with the consensus EPS estimate being $6.52.

While investors scrutinize revenue and earnings changes year-over-year and how they compare with Wall Street expectations to determine their next move, some key metrics always offer a more accurate picture of a company's financial health.

As these metrics influence top- and bottom-line performance, comparing them to the year-ago numbers and what analysts estimated helps investors project a stock's price performance more accurately.

Headcount : 66,775 compared to the 69,468 average estimate based on four analysts.

Advertising Revenue- US & Canada : $28.44 billion versus the four-analyst average estimate of $27.64 billion. The reported number represents a year-over-year change of +33.3%.

Geographical Revenue by User- US & Canada : $28.91 billion compared to the $28.07 billion average estimate based on four analysts. The reported number represents a change of +32.9% year over year.

news.Title: Meta Platforms Q3 Earnings Call Highlights
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in Meta Platforms, Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

Meta's Q3 revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion , driven by stronger advertising demand, higher engagement and AI-enhanced recommendations across its apps. Ad impressions increased 10%, while average ad prices rose 14%.

Expenses surged 68% to $51.6 billion, including a $9.9 billion legal charge and continued AI infrastructure spending. Capital expenditures reached $34.9 billion, pushing free cash flow to negative $2.1 billion.

Meta highlighted rapid adoption of its Muse AI agent and expects to develop future revenue through commerce fees, subscriptions, APIs and business services. The company forecast Q4 revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion and announced an effective two-for-one stock split expected to begin trading in late January 2027.

Synchrony Aces The Quarter As Credit Fears Fade

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) reported third-quarter 2026 revenue growth of 26% as advertising demand, engagement gains and AI-driven improvements across its apps supported results, while expenses rose sharply due to a nearly $10 billion legal charge and continued infrastructure investment.

Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg said Meta's family of apps reached 3.64 billion daily users during the quarter. Facebook and Instagram posted all-time highs in engagement, driven largely by video, while Threads surpassed X in monthly active users, according to Zuckerberg. WhatsApp also reached all-time highs in messaging activity.

→ The AI Sell-Off Continues—These 3 Stocks Keep Raising Guidance Anyway

The AI Buildout Is Only 15% Complete—Here Is Where the Next Dollar Actually Goes

The company reported total revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26% from a year earlier on both a reported and constant-currency basis. Family of Apps revenue was $64.2 billion, including $63.1 billion in advertising revenue, which also rose 26%.

Total expenses increased 68% to $51.6 billion, including a $9.9 billion charge related to Meta's August 2026 agreement with multiple state attorneys general. GAAP operating income fell 37% to $13 billion, while the operating margin was 20%. Excluding the legal charge, Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said operating income would have risen 11% year over year.

→ Tesla's Roadster Reveal Hints at 2 Much Bigger Moves

Meta Platforms' AI Comeback Faces an Earnings Test—And a $10 Billion Charge

Net income was $9.9 billion, or $3.83 per share. Capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, reached $34.9 billion as Meta invested in servers, data centers and network infrastructure. Free cash flow was negative $2.1 billion for the quarter.

Story Continues

Advertising and engagement trends

Meta said ad impressions delivered across its services increased 10% year over year, while the global average price per ad rose 14%. Li attributed pricing gains to better ad performance and improved macroeconomic conditions compared with the prior-year period, partially offset by impression growth in lower-monetizing regions and surfaces.

→ Luxury's Middle Market Is Cracking—These 3 Stocks Could Win

Meta continued to emphasize the role of AI in improving content recommendations and ad performance. On Instagram, global time spent per user reached an all-time high and rose by double digits year over year, with growth in both Reels and Feed. Facebook Reels time spent also reached all-time highs globally and in the U.S.

Li said Instagram Reels relevance initiatives introduced during the quarter lifted Reels time spent by more than 4%. On Facebook, a new generative retrieval architecture was deployed to about one-quarter of unconnected Feed views and half of Reels views, contributing a 1% increase in Reels watch time.

In advertising, Meta said its Meta Generative Recommender system drove a nearly 2% increase in conversions across targeted Facebook Feed segments. The company also expanded its GEM ad-ranking model, which increased conversions by 1.7% for off-site conversion campaigns and 9.6% for app-ad conversion campaigns, according to Li.

Meta's AI Business Assistant has also become a more active tool for advertisers. The company estimated that advertisers adopting its recommendations generated nearly 5% more conversions at the same cost per conversion and increased advertising spending by 9% relative to similar non-adopters.

Nearly 10 million advertisers used at least one of Meta's generative AI advertising tools in the third quarter. Meanwhile, partnership ads surpassed a $15 billion annual revenue run rate after growing more than 97% year over year, Li said.

Muse agent expansion and monetization plans

Zuckerberg focused much of the call on Muse, Meta's personal AI agent. He said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up Muse agents in roughly six weeks. About 25% of people who have set up Muse use it on a given day, according to Zuckerberg.

Shopping has been the most common Muse use case, with more than one-quarter of active users engaging in shopping and an average purchase size above $200. Zuckerberg later clarified that the commerce data includes travel purchases. Personal productivity and connections to services such as email and calendars were also among the leading use cases.

Meta has not yet launched Muse globally, with Zuckerberg citing the service's compute intensity, the need for regional product optimization and the company's desire to improve efficiency before broader expansion. Meta expects to improve Muse compute-cost efficiency by more than tenfold over the next year through measures including more efficient models, inference optimization and use of off-peak capacity.

The company expects Muse to remain free for most users, with revenue eventually generated through commerce fees paid by businesses, paid subscriptions for advanced models or additional token usage, and subscriptions for business features and workplace uses. Zuckerberg said the company plans to build enough capacity to serve more than 1 billion people over the next several years.

Meta is also developing enterprise offerings around its models, including an API, Muse Code and business agents. Li said Meta believes AI could create a diversified recurring revenue stream through subscriptions, usage-based APIs, messaging and other revenue sources, though the opportunity is expected to develop over multiple years.

Reality Labs, outlook and capital structure

Reality Labs revenue declined 6% to $443 million, as lower Quest headset sales were partially offset by growth in AI glasses revenue. Zuckerberg said Muse will begin coming to Meta Glasses next month and that the company expects subscriptions tied to glasses to increase.

Meta expects Reality Labs operating losses to decline to about $15 billion next year, following expected 2026 losses of $18 billion to $19 billion. Zuckerberg said the company is pacing virtual-reality investment more selectively and prioritizing personal-superintelligence initiatives.

Fourth-quarter 2026 revenue is expected to be between $73 billion and $76 billion.

Full-year 2026 expenses are expected to total $175 billion to $179 billion, including the legal charge.

Full-year 2026 capital expenditures are forecast at $135 billion to $145 billion.

Meta expects foreign exchange to represent an approximately 1% headwind to fourth-quarter year-over-year revenue growth.

The company ended the quarter with $82.4 billion in cash and marketable securities and $83.7 billion in debt. Meta also announced plans to create a new class of non-voting capital stock that will be distributed as a stock dividend, giving shareholders one non-voting share for each existing share held. The move effectively represents a two-for-one stock split, with trading expected to begin in late January 2027.

About Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META)

Meta Platforms, Inc is a technology company that develops social networking, messaging, virtual and augmented reality, and artificial intelligence products. The company's principal platforms include Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, WhatsApp, and Threads, which enable users to connect, communicate, share content, and discover products and services.

Meta also operates Reality Labs, its division focused on virtual, augmented, and mixed reality technologies. Reality Labs develops products such as Meta Quest virtual reality headsets and related software and experiences, along with research and hardware intended to support immersive computing.

news.Title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty to New Mexico in data privacy case
news.Content:
By Diana Novak Jones

Oct 21 (Reuters) - A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.

The ruling came in a ‌case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their ‌consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.

"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the ​heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.

Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.

In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new ‌rules for what people can say online."

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl ⁠Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.

Meta previously faced a $5 billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related ⁠to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health.

LAWSUIT FILED FIVE YEARS AGO

New Mexico's attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users ​in ​New Mexico about who had access to their data and its handling of hate speech and misinformation posted ​on the platform. It alleged the company knew third parties had broad ‌access to users' data and tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line.

Story Continues

Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting.

"It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers."

Mathew's decision comes as Meta faces thousands of lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers over the impact of Instagram and Facebook on teen mental health, with another trial slated to begin next week.

Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942 million in a pair of trials against Meta over ‌claims it facilitated sexual exploitation of young people on Instagram and Facebook and misled consumers about the ​platforms' safety.

Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the latest New Mexico ruling costly ​but unlikely to impact the company's value.

"Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and ​will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said.

EXPERTS EXPECT LONG APPEAL FIGHT

Jurors in September had found that the company and ‌its leadership made 26 misleading statements on data privacy, hate speech and ​other subjects. Multiplying those statements by their potential ​audience, they said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws.

At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion.

"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the ​value of its stock price," McGinn said.

In court filings, Meta urged ‌Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had ​actually been misled, the company said in court filings.

(Reporting by Diana Novak Jones in Chicago, additional reporting by Andrew Hay in New Mexico and Jaspreet Singh ​and Anzar Mehraj in Bangalore. Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Nia Williams, Aurora Ellis and Stephen Coates)

news.Title: Citadel's Ken Griffin Makes Stark Call on AI Boom
news.Content: This article first appeared on GuruFocus . Citadel founder Ken Griffin says investors are almost certainly in the middle of an artificial intelligence bubble , even as he believes the technology could reshape the economy and create a new generation of dominant companies. Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with AMZN. Is AMZN fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator. Griffin said the biggest problem is that corporate America is still struggling to prove that enormous AI spending is producing enough economic value. Corporate America has been very uneven in its ability to extract value from its AI models, Griffin said at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York. He added that companies are increasingly looking at their bills from OpenAI and Anthropic and asking whether the productivity gains justify the cost. That question is becoming more important as spending on AI infrastructure continues to soar. Amazon ( NASDAQ:AMZN ) backed Anthropic, which is expected to file for an IPO in the coming weeks, could spend as much as $750 billion on additional computing power in the years ahead , according to The Wall Street Journal. Griffin said Anthropic's long-term success will depend on proving that its models become indispensable across industries. But his warning is not the same as saying AI is a fad. Any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble, Griffin said. He compared the current environment with the dot-com era, when investors poured money into companies with weak or speculative business models even as the internet itself went on to transform the global economy. Investor Takeaway I think Griffin's point is more nuanced than simply calling AI overvalued. He is effectively saying the technology can be transformative while the capital flowing into it is still excessive . That distinction matters. The biggest risk may not be that AI demand disappears. It is that too many companies are being valued as if they will all become long-term winners. History suggests they will not. Griffin also believes AI could threaten white-collar jobs and established competitive advantages while simultaneously creating what he called a golden era for entrepreneurs. For investors, the key things to watch are AI monetization, enterprise productivity gains, infrastructure spending, cash burn and whether companies can convert usage into durable profits . If Griffin is right, the AI boom could still create enormous winners. But some of today's valuations may not survive the journey. news.Title: Buying This Stock Right Now Could Be a Once-in-a-Generation Opportunity
news.Content:
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL) is emerging as one of the biggest beneficiaries of a major shift in artificial intelligence infrastructure . Its latest growth projections suggest that the company could be significantly larger in just a few years.

Management recently raised its fiscal 2028 revenue outlook to approximately $20 billion, up from its previous forecast of $18 billion. That's a massive number for a company that generated $8.2 billion in fiscal 2026. Marvell is now also targeting $70 billion to $90 billion in annual revenue by fiscal 2031, with much of that growth expected to come from custom AI chips and data center networking.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The custom chip advantage

Today, companies such as Microsoft , Amazon , and Alphabet 's Google rely heavily on Nvidia 's graphics processing units (GPUs) to run their AI systems. The tech giants are increasingly developing chips specifically designed for their own workloads. These custom chips, known as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), can deliver better efficiency and lower costs for certain AI applications.

Marvell helps develop these chips. It also supplies networking technology that allows thousands of processors to communicate inside enormous AI data centers. Demand is accelerating rapidly. In fact, Marvell's data center business is now the company's largest revenue contributor.

A once-in-a-generation opportunity

If Marvell reaches $80 billion in annual revenue by fiscal 2031, the midpoint of management's target, its business would be nearly 10 times larger than it was in fiscal 2026. Management has also projected approximately $30 in adjusted earnings per share by fiscal 2031. Assuming Marvell can deliver those earnings and investors are willing to pay 25 times annual profits (a valuation that could be reasonable for a rapidly growing AI semiconductor company), its stock could reach approximately $750. That's more than triple its recent price of $237.

Of course, there's still some risk. Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) is a powerful competitor you can't ignore, and AI infrastructure spending could slow. But if you're willing to hold for several years and tolerate a bit of volatility, Marvell could indeed prove to be a once-in-a-generation opportunity.

Prediction: This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Will Be the Biggest Winner of 2027
news.Content:
In my view, artificial intelligence (AI) stocks will once again lead the market higher in 2027. However, I think there will start to be a rotation away from the pure-play pick-and-shovel infrastructure players and toward the hyperscalers that control the bulk of the spending. And against that backdrop, I think Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) is poised to be the best performing stock among AI mega-caps in 2027.

Whenever a new technological evolution is in its early phases, a large fraction of the gains go to the hardware companies that lay the foundation for it. However, in later stages, the gains should increasingly go to the companies that are benefiting from the prior investments.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

This pattern could certainly be seen in the dot-com boom. Hardware giants like Cisco , Sun Microsystems, and JDS Uniphase led the early build-out, but companies like Amazon and Google (now Alphabet) were the ones that captured the vast majority of the cumulative economic value over the long run.

I think a similar dynamic should start to play out again beginning next year, with Alphabet in position to be the clearest beneficiary. One of the biggest differences between the dot-com era and the AI era is that some of the companies funding the current build-out are the same ones building the end-user applications and platform ecosystems. Back in the late 1990s, it was telecoms that were doing most of the heavy lifting on infrastructure, while today it is the hyperscalers themselves. That is also one of the big reasons why these companies have been increasingly designing their own chips, and this is where Alphabet shines.

During the early phases of a new infrastructure build-out, there typically are large supply-and-demand imbalances. In this case, that gave semiconductor companies massive pricing power. The greatest example of this can be seen in the memory market, where prices have skyrocketed to unprecedented heights due to the shortage of memory chips. However, over time, supply chains normalize, production catches up to demand, and hardware prices come down. Investors have already started pricing in the potential of this happening.

Multiple advantages

In this middle phase that we are entering now, Alphabet has the biggest advantage because it has designed its entire ecosystem around its powerful custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). These processors give it a huge cost advantage in training its own AI models and running inference workloads. They also provide it with the strongest long-term cloud computing economics.

Story Continues

When using its own chips, Alphabet is getting a payback on its chip investments in about a year, compared to two to three years for rival hyperscaler Amazon. Meanwhile, a one-year payback on custom compute allows Alphabet to reinvest its operational cash flow back into data center expansion much faster than peers that are more reliant on Nvidia 's graphics processing units (GPUs) and therefore face longer payback horizons. Its chips are so highly regarded that, in association with its design partner, Broadcom , it is also selling them directly to compute-starved Anthropic, giving it another high-margin revenue stream.

Ultimately, Alphabet is poised to be one of the biggest AI winners because it controls every single layer of the AI stack. This starts with its custom chips, then moves to it having its own top-tier AI model, Gemini. Alphabet also has its own cloud platform (Vertex AI) and its own cloud security solution (Wiz). Alphabet then has the important product layer with Google Search, YouTube, and its other apps, where it can incorporate its Gemini model to improve its products and drive growth.

Alphabet also controls a large piece of the distribution layer through its ownership of the Chrome browser and the Android operating system, to go along with its revenue-sharing agreement for Google Search to be the default search engine on Apple devices. This essentially makes it the gateway to the internet and, increasingly, AI. And finally, it also controls the ad layer, as its ad network makes it easier to monetize consumer AI.

Altogether, this gives it the ultimate AI flywheel, and the value of that should start to shine through even more next year. That's why I think Alphabet will be the best-performing mega-cap AI stock in 2027.

news.Title: Trading Day: Tech it away
news.Content:
By Jamie McGeever

ORLANDO, Florida, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Buoyant AI sentiment on the back of quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer lifted Wall Street on Wednesday, as relatively calm energy, currency, and US bond markets allowed tech earnings to dominate. European markets were more lively, however, and France's 10-year bond yield rose above 5% ‌for the first time in nearly a quarter of a century.

In my column today, I look at five AI quirks and conundrums that investors should be aware of as ‌the US earnings season gets underway.

Today's Key Reads

• Government websites go dark as software flaw sparks security scramble

• Anthropic logged net loss of over $80 billion in first half of 2026

• Smouldering debt risk haunts French markets: Mike Dolan

• UK inflation ​and borrowing climb before Healey's first budget

• Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico after jury finds company misled consumers about data privacy

• Today's Key Market Moves STOCKS: South Korea +3.3%, best day since September 7. Europe +1%, UK steady. Mexico +1.5%. Nasdaq +1%, Dow +0.7%, S&P 500 +0.6%.SECTORS/SHARES: Seven sectors on the S&P 500 rise, four fall. Tech +1.6%, communications services -1.3%. Meta +4% after the bell on earnings, Tesla +2%, IBM +7%.FX: US dollar steady. Biggest G10 gainer is Aussie dollar, Indian rupee rises to six-week high. Biggest decliner Mexican peso, -1.5%.BONDS: French 10-year yield hits 5% for first time since 2002. US 20-year auction mixed — 2.73 bid/cover at the higher end of range of ‌the last year, but highest auction yield since 1986, some analysts ⁠say.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil mixed — Brent steady, WTI settles lower. Gold little changed at $4,135/oz.

Today's Talking Points:

Anthropic

AI leader Anthropic posted a whopping $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of this year. That was up significantly from a $13 billion loss a year earlier, largely due to a $72 billion accounting charge. The net loss is almost ⁠double the $42 billion loss reported for calendar year 2025. Revenue in the first six months of the year was just over $16 billion.

Are these figures bullish or bearish? Depends which camp you're in. The headline loss is alarming, but it was mainly due to a one-off charge. Revenue is low and growth is slowing, but exclude the accounting charge and break-even doesn't look quite so far away. However, are the numbers and trends those ​of ​a company eyeing a $1.5-$2 trillion IPO valuation?

Sub subprime

Is the US housing market frozen? It's certainly seizing up, which ​is traditionally a major red flag for the wider economy. Pending home sales ‌in September plunged to the lowest since records began a quarter of a century ago, and housing starts fell 5.2% in the month to their lowest since the pandemic. US homebuilder sentiment, meanwhile, has plunged to the lowest level in nearly 14-1/2 years.

Story Continues

Rising Fed interest rates, stubbornly high home prices, and mortgage rates the highest in three years at 7.50% are all factors. But it is remarkable that activity now is even weaker than it was at the heights — or depths? — of the 2008 US housing market crash and its aftermath, and the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020. Given the importance of housing and related services to the US economy, growth could suffer.

Pounding the beat

UK finance minister John Healey delivers his first budget next week. To say he faces a few challenges would be an ‌understatement. Figures this week show government borrowing in September rose more than expected again, and public debt surpassed ​the psychologically key £3 trillion mark. Part of the reason why borrowing last month rose so much was debt interest payments — ​bond yields are the highest in decades, and with the debt pile growing, it's a ​difficult cycle to get out of. He has little wiggle room next week.

Bad news for sterling, right? Not necessarily. The latest inflation and wage growth data ‌have cemented market expectations for a rate hike on November 5. Indeed, ​traders now reckon the Bank of England will be ​the most hawkish G10 central bank over the next year or so, along with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, and raise rates more than 100 bps. Sterling has pounced on the euro's weakness, surging almost 3% in the last month to its highest since May last year. And cable is rebounding from its year low. Next stop $1.35?

What could move ​markets tomorrow?

• New Zealand inflation (September)

• South Korea interest rate decision

• Canada PPI ‌inflation (September)

• US Treasury sells $26 billion of 5-year TIPS

• US earnings including Procter & Gamble, Union Pacific, Western Digital, Lockheed Martin

Want to receive Trading Day in your inbox every weekday ​morning? Sign up for my newsletter here. Opinions expressed are those of the author. They do not reflect the views of Reuters News, which, under the Trust ​Principles, is committed to integrity, independence, and freedom from bias.

(Reporting by Jamie McGeever; Editing by Nia Williams)

news.Title: Q3 Earnings Beats for Meta, Tesla, IBM and T.I.
news.Content:
Mag 7 companies are now being heard from in Q3 earnings season. Meta Platforms META — parent company of Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger and Threads — outpaced estimates on both top and bottom lines after the closing bell today. Earnings of $3.83 per share surpassed the $3.45 analysts were looking for, on revenues of $64.6 billion in the quarter, its highest ever, and up +26% year over year.

Earnings were still well off the pace set in the year-ago quarter, and that's because Meta was hit with a $10 billion charge (of an $18 billion settlement overall) in a multi-state deal regarding social media addiction in young people. Revenue guidance was increased to a $73-76 billion range for the current quarter, as the company also projects between $135-145 billion in additional capex spending on AI infrastructure.

Finally, the company is rewarding shareholders with a 2-for-1 stock split. META stock is up +3.9% on the news in late trading, adding to its slim +5.67% gains year to date.

Tesla TSLA also outperformed the Zacks consensus on earnings and revenues, with $0.48 per share coming in 3 cents higher than estimates on revenues of $28.05 billion, beating the $27.78 billion estimate. Auto Gross Margins (minus EV credits) were up +18.1%, better than analysts had projected. Full-Service Driving (ESD) subscriptions rose +67% year over year to 1.74 million in the quarter.The Tesla robotaxi has now clocked 2 million unsupervised miles, and its Optimus robot production has begun at its Fremont, CA auto plant.

It's been a busy week for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who saw his SpaceX SPCX Q3 numbers skyrocket (no pun intended) after Tuesday's close. He has also been implicated in the Starlink slowdown in Ukraine that hampered the U.S. ally's ability to conduct its war against Russia. Tesla shares are up +1.4% in late trading, but still down more than -12% year to date.

IBM Corp. IBM kept the Q3 tech earnings beats alight this afternoon, with earnings of $2.95 per share surpassed the $2.88 in the Zacks consensus on $17.10 billion in revenues, which beat the $16.87 billion forecast. Software and Infrastructure revenues beat consensus estimates, and the tech giant is looking for full-year revenue growth of between 4-5%. IBM shares are up +3.5% in the after-market.

Zacks Rank #2 (Buy)-rated Texas Instruments TXN came in well ahead of expectations on its Q3 bottom line after today's close: $2.62 per share versus $2.40 estimated. Revenues of $6.06 billion improved over the $5.93 billion analysts were looking for. Analog revenues and guidance numbers came in better than expected. Investors are selling the news a bit, sending shares down marginally after +64% gains year to date.

news.Title: Bank of America sees a $300 billion test for Google stock
news.Content:
Google has a massive $300 billion question hanging over its lofty AI ambitions, and Bank of America thinks investors need to pay attention.

That's roughly the amount of money the bank expects Alphabet ( GOOGL ) to spend on capital expenditures in 2027, building data centers and AI chips.

Take something as familiar as searching for a restaurant. Over the past several years, Google has steered you toward reviews, menus, and reservation pages. Now, its AI tools can pull together answers and recommendations before you ever click through.

Though that feels like a small convenience. Behind the scenes, though, providing those answers entails costly chips and data centers. And as people's search habits change, Google needs to find ways to keep its lucrative advertising business growing.

That's quite a balancing act, which involves paying for the future without weakening the business financing it.

That said, in a note shared with me, Bank of America remains bullish, maintaining a Buy rating and $430 price target. However, the company's CapEx forecast raises a big question for shareholders: whether Google's growing AI and cloud businesses can generate enough cash to justify the bill.

Bank of America sees Google's cloud growth masking a costly problem

On the surface, it's easy to see why Google will continue on an upward trajectory.

More Google:

Google is making a change in November that might catch Gemini users off guard

Google set to challenge Meta Muse in the Agentic AI race

Google just disclosed something troubling about its AI

Alphabet brought in $119.8 billion in Q2 sales , up 24% from a year earlier. Google Cloud, once a smaller piece of the business, grew 82% to $24.8 billion, an extraordinary pace for a company of Google's size.

Post expects the momentum to continue when Alphabet reports on October 28. His Q3 forecast calls for $111.4 billion in sales after traffic-acquisition costs and $3.07 in GAAP earnings per share, ahead of Wall Street's comparable estimates of $111 billion and $2.98.

That said, the growth isn't evenly spread across Google.

Bank of America expects Search revenue growth to cool from 17% in the previous quarter to 14%, while Cloud accelerates from 82% to 93%. Google's traditional cash-generating business is growing much more slowly, even as its AI infrastructure operations expand rapidly.

The more surprising finding is BofA's cash-flow forecast.

The bank expects negative free cash flow of $12.4 billion in Q3, compared with about $3.9 billion expected by other analysts. And it forecasts around $300 billion in capital spending in 2027 alone.

Story Continues

That's a huge financial balancing act. Google can continue to deliver strong sales, even blow past earnings estimates, while pouring more cash into the data centers powering its AI ambitions.

So why is a business this profitable consuming so much cash?

Google's AI ambitions could consume $500 billion in just two years

BofA expects Google's AI ambitions to come with a massive bill.

It estimates Alphabet will spend about $199 billion in CapEx in 2026 and another $301 billion in 2027. That's roughly half a trillion dollars in just two years, much of it tied to data centers, computing chips, and the infrastructure needed to handle rising AI demand.

But Google isn't simply buying more servers and hoping customers show up.

It's building its own Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), expanding cloud capacity, and selling computing power and AI services to other businesses.

Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian offered a sense of that demand at a September technology conference.

He said over 300 customers had each committed over $100 million, while customers were spending, on average, more than 50% above their contractual commitments.

Kurian also said Google's AI servers pay for themselves in under two years, with its own TPUs expected to pay back faster than conventional graphics processors.

Nevertheless, there are a few caveats to consider.

Bank of America notes that an index tracking AI-model usage costs fell 33% in Q3. Cheaper AI might attract more customers, but Google needs enough additional usage to offset the lower per-unit earnings.

And its original moneymaker faces a different challenge.

As Google adds AI answers and rivals develop agents that complete tasks directly, users might have fewer reasons to visit websites. Pew Research found traditional search-result clicks occurred in 8% of visits with AI summaries, versus 15% without them.

So even though Google has the customers and technology to make this work. Whether they can generate enough cash to justify the bill is another matter.

Buffett's big Google bet faces an October 28 reality check

Interestingly, that question also matters to Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A), too.

Years ago, Buffett admitted he'd missed an opportunity in Google's advertising business, despite the potential it saw through GEICO's search-ad spending as reported on CNBC . He eventually initiated Berkshire Hathaway's Alphabet investment, just as Google was becoming a much more expensive business to build, which I covered a few months ago .

Now, investors have an important date circled which is when Alphabet reports earnings on October 28 for Q3 .

Bank of America expects Google Cloud revenue to grow 93%. But another impressive growth number won't settle the debate.

Investors will want to know whether Search advertising is holding up as AI changes how people find information, and whether Google can turn soaring Cloud demand into stronger margins.

Then there's the spending. Any increase in Alphabet's CapEx outlook, or a deeper free cash flow shortfall, would raise fresh questions about how quickly its AI investments can pay off.

Even headline earnings may need a closer look.

BofA estimates Alphabet's SpaceX stake could produce a significant mark-to-market headwind, complicating comparisons with the unusually large investment gains recorded earlier this year.

The big new challenge is whether those businesses can generate enough cash over the coming years to support the extraordinary infrastructure being built around them.

news.Title: $4,000 in These 4 Non-Nvidia Chip Stocks Could Be Worth This Much by 2030
news.Content:
Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) is now the largest company on the planet; its market cap represents around 7.5% of the value of the S&P 500 . As such, if you own any mutual funds or exchange-traded funds (ETFs) -- particularly index funds -- you probably already have a lot of exposure to the giant chipmaker.

However, if you want to build a small portfolio of other chip stocks, you could do so by buying a basket that includes Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), Marvell (NASDAQ: MRVL), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD), and Arm Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM). Splitting an initial investment of around $4,000 fairly evenly, you could buy three shares of Broadcom, four shares of Marvell, two shares of AMD, and four shares of Arm. And if the AI infrastructure boom continues, by 2030, that semiconductor portfolio could be worth over $10,000. That's about a 150% return. Here's how.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Broadcom and Marvell

One of the biggest trends in AI infrastructure now is that hyperscalers (owners of large data centers) are choosing to designing custom parallel processors that are narrowly suited to their own computing needs. These application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) -- hardwired chips built for specific tasks -- can lower costs and improve cloud computing and data center economics.

However, hyperscalers generally need the intellectual property and know-how of companies that specialize in this tech niche to turn their concepts into complete designs, and as such, they are increasingly turning to Broadcom and Marvell. Broadcom counts Alphabet , Anthropic, Meta Platforms , and OpenAI among its customers, while Amazon and Microsoft are Marvell's custom chip customers. This is a huge and growing business for both companies.

Analysts are forecasting that Broadcom's adjusted earnings per share (EPS) will grow to $52.15 in its fiscal 2031 (which ends in October 2031). The S&P 500 currently has a forward P/E of around 19 times; if you apply that multiple to Broadcom's fiscal 2031 consensus EPS estimate, the stock would trade at roughly $990 in late 2030. As such, your three-share investment would approximately triple in value to nearly $3,000.

Apply a similar multiple to the $40.93 consensus expectation for Marvell's EPS in fiscal 2032 (which ends in January 2032), and that stock would trade at nearly $780 at the end of 2030. Your four shares would have more than tripled in price to be worth around $3,100.

Story Continues

AMD and Arm

AMD and Arm are plays on the expected rise of AI agents and the corresponding surge in demand for data center central processing units (CPUs). While servers dedicated to training AI only needed one CPU for every eight to 16 graphics processing units (GPUs), those that will power AI agents need equal numbers of CPUs and GPUs. AMD has said it sees the data center CPU market growing in size to $220 billion by 2030. AMD is a leader in this space, while Arm's technology has long been used in advanced custom CPUs. However, given the size of the opportunity, Arm will also start making its own chips for the first time.

AMD also has a big opportunity in the AI inference space with its GPUs. It has large commitments from OpenAI, Meta Platforms, and Anthropic to buy those processors -- deals that should also drive its growth in the coming years.

Analysts currently project AMD's 2030 EPS will come in at $44.31. Assume another 20% growth in 2031, and that would bring its 2031 EPS target to $53.14. That's a big jump from the $7.59 per share that analysts expect it to earn this year. Place a 19-times-forward-earnings multiple on the stock, and it would be worth $1,010 at the end of 2030. That's nearly double the current stock price, and a two-share stake would be worth $2,020.

The current consensus for Arm's fiscal 2032 (ending March 2032) adjusted EPS, meanwhile, is $11.98. The stock has always traded at a large premium due to its licensing and subscription model, although as it shifts to a hybrid model that also includes the sale of its own chips, that premium should come down. If we apply a 40-times forward P/E to the stock (down from over 100), it would trade at roughly $480. That's more than a twofold increase, and four shares would be worth around $1,920.

Add it all up, and your $4,000 investment made today would be worth about $10,000 four years from now.

news.Title: Amazon or Alphabet: If I Could Only Own One for the Next Decade, It Would Be This One
news.Content:
Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) are two companies that hardly need an introduction. Both are leaders in their respective industries, generally post excellent financial results, and have crushed broader equities over the long run. Investors arguably can't go wrong with either of these, and I personally own shares of both. But if I had to pick just one to own for the next decade, it would likely be Alphabet. Here's why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The AI tailwind could favor Alphabet

Over the next 10 years, the cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) industries will likely continue growing. Amazon and Alphabet, two leaders in these markets, are both likely to capitalize. What separates the two companies? Let's start with Amazon. The company's cloud segment, Amazon Web Services (AWS), boasts the largest market share.

Amazon offers perhaps the largest library of services among the Big Three in the cloud computing industry. However, Alphabet is particularly competitive in the AI niche of the cloud market. Alphabet's cloud sales have been growing faster in recent quarters. During the second quarter, Google Cloud's revenue soared by 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. Alphabet's total revenue jumped by 24% year over year to $119.8 billion.

By contrast, Amazon's total revenue increased 20% year over year to $200.6 billion, with AWS cloud sales jumping 37% year over year to $42.2 billion. One reason I'd pick Alphabet over Amazon right now is the former's strength in AI. Despite fears that the AI bubble will burst, spending on the technology continues to rise, and we are arguably just entering the era of agentic AI systems.

There is at least some evidence that demand for agentic AI is there. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) launched one of the first consumer-facing AI agents in September, and it has been hugely successful so far. Corporations are also extensively using AI agents. And as more of them are developed, demand for precisely the sort of services that Alphabet and Amazon offer should continue to rise. All that to say, bullish long-term projections about AI infrastructure spending appear justified, and Alphabet is in a particularly strong position to capitalize on that.

Margins matter

What if we look at the rest of their businesses? Amazon's is larger, at least in terms of sales. But Alphabet has an advantage. Its business carries much higher margins. That's not surprising. Alphabet makes most of its money from digital ads (Amazon's ad business is much smaller than Alphabet's). Once the advertising infrastructure is up and running, the cost of showing one additional ad is small. Meanwhile, Amazon's core e-commerce business is a famously low-margin operation.

Story Continues

In fairness, the company is looking to improve on that front, and in my view, it will succeed. Amazon has launched AI-powered robots in its warehouses to help streamline the packaging and shipping process. That's one of the initiatives the company has implemented to improve e-commerce margins. Still, for now, Alphabet has a clear advantage in this category.

As a result, despite generating lower sales, Alphabet typically records higher profits.

GOOGL Revenue (Annual) data by YCharts

E-commerce and digital advertising are both industries with attractive long-term growth prospects, and given their wide moats, Amazon and Alphabet are likely to remain leaders in their respective markets. Over the long run, Alphabet's earnings could remain higher than Amazon's due to its higher-margin core business.

What about valuation?

Even with its fast-growing cloud business, strong margins, high profits, and attractive long-term prospects, Alphabet appears to be reasonably valued. The company is trading at 21.8x forward earnings. True, that's a bit higher than the 19.1x average for information technology stocks, but Alphabet is worth a premium considering the strength of its business.

Amazon also looks attractively valued. It is trading at 23.6x forward earnings, compared to the 23.3x average for consumer discretionary stocks. Perhaps if Amazon were deeply undervalued relative to its growth potential -- and by comparison with Alphabet -- it'd be the better stock to buy today. But that's not the case. It's another reason why I'd choose Alphabet, but again, that's only if I absolutely had to pick one of them. I'd advise investors to buy shares of both companies.

news.Title: Is STMicroelectronics (STM) a Buy Heading Into Earnings?
news.Content:
STMicroelectronics (NYSE:STM) reports third-quarter results next week, and the company has already set the bar. It guided to revenue of about $3.70 billion, up about 16.2% from a year earlier, and a gross margin near 37.0%. STMicroelectronics is one of the 8 Best NYSE Stocks with Huge Upside Potential .

That growth rate is slower than the 26.0% it posted in the second quarter, which is the first surprise. The bigger question is whether profit will follow. STMicroelectronics sells chips used in cars and other electronics, and it now says AI data centers and satellite networks will drive its next leg up. Sales are clearly recovering, but earnings are lagging, and the stock's price assumes they catch up.

Sales Have Snapped Back From a Long Slump

Growth was hard to find for years, with revenue falling about 9.8% a year over the past three years and growing only about 2.9% a year over five. Then second-quarter revenue rose 26.0% from a year earlier. Management said bookings were strong in every end market, and its embedded processing unit grew fastest, led by general-purpose microcontrollers.

That rebound matters because it shows demand coming back across the business, not in one corner of it. If you're interested in high-growth chip stocks, we recently compiled a report on 12 High Growth Semiconductor Stocks to Buy Now .

Stocks chart

AI Data Centers and Satellites Add New Demand

Management has raised its targets for the new businesses. At the first-quarter report, STMicroelectronics expected data center revenue nicely above $500 million for 2026 and well above $1 billion for 2027. At the second-quarter report, it lifted those to above $1 billion for 2026 and well above $2 billion for 2027.

Chief Executive Jean-Marc Chery also told investors to expect growth to speed up in the fourth quarter, mainly from AI data center and low-earth-orbit satellite programs with customers already engaged. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue above $4 billion. That means growth slows in the third quarter before it picks up again. For investors looking to own the AI chip trade for years, our list of 10 Best AI Chip Stocks to Buy for the Long Term is worth a look.

Profit Is Still Trailing Sales

Profit is the weak spot, and the second-quarter operating margin shows it. It was 5.4% under U.S. GAAP, up from the first quarter but still thin next to that sales growth. The figure also carried $58 million of impairment, restructuring and phase-out costs from the company's plan to reshape its factory footprint.

Story Continues

Cash flow looks better than earnings do. Free cash flow was positive at $75 million in the second quarter, against a negative $152 million a year earlier, even as the company kept spending heavily on factories. Charges for unused factory capacity also fell from the first quarter to the second, while management said demand kept rising in the quarter.

The third-quarter gross margin target already includes a drag from that unused capacity, so the company is guiding to progress even with the cost in. For shareholders, margin is what decides whether faster sales turn into earnings. A gross margin that lands near 37.0% would back the recovery story, and a miss would raise doubts about it.

What the Price Already Assumes

STMicroelectronics trades at about 34 times forward earnings, a multiple built on adjusted figures. The sector median is about 21.5 times, and the company's own five-year average is about 22.8 times. Adjusted earnings matter here, because second-quarter net income was $291 million on an adjusted basis and $222 million under U.S. GAAP.

The price is betting that the recovery lifts earnings well beyond what the reported numbers show today. If you're looking for cheaper growth ideas, check out 10 Undervalued Growth Stocks to Buy Now .

So profits are following sales, but only partly. Operating margin has risen from the first quarter, yet it remains thin next to the rebound, and a valuation this far above its history needs that gap to close. The report next week will show whether gross margin reaches that target and whether management still sees fourth-quarter revenue above $4 billion.

While we acknowledge the risk and potential of STM as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. news.Title: Microsoft Must Say This on Oct. 28 or the Stock Will Go Into Free Fall
news.Content:
Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) has a major event coming up on Oct. 28: its earnings report for its fiscal 2027 first quarter, which ended Sept. 30. The tech giant has had an OK year overall. The stock started off calendar 2026 in a steady decline that sapped about 25% from its starting price by late March, rebounded partway, and then sank back to that low level again in June. But since then, it has sustained a rally and is now up about 10% for the year, though that still trails the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), which is up by almost 13%.

The question is whether Microsoft can finish the year strong or if there's another sell-off waiting in the wings. I think we'll get more clarity on that when it next reports results.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Azure's growth will be in focus

Microsoft is a massive tech company that does a lot of things, but at this point, there's really only one that matters: AI. There are essentially three legs to its AI strategy: Copilot, Azure, and its investment in and partnership with OpenAI.

The investment in OpenAI has made Microsoft a ton of money, and when the AI lab eventually goes public, that will put a huge gain on Microsoft's books. But that won't happen until 2027 at the earliest.

Copilot, Microsoft's internal generative AI platform that can interface with its Office productivity suite, also offers huge growth potential. In the company's fiscal 2026 Q4, which ended June 30, Copilot crossed 30 million paid seats. Its impressive growth is helping drive Microsoft's overall growth in its productivity and business processes segment.

However, I'd argue that its most important segment is Azure, its cloud computing platform. While Copilot and its OpenAI investment have the potential to make Microsoft a fair bit of money, they pale in comparison to what Azure can do. Azure is the key to Microsoft's future, but some red flags are starting to appear.

Azure's growth rate hasn't taken off like its peers

Azure will see a greater growth rate than most of Microsoft's other AI endeavors because it's attracting many different AI start-ups. It's the service that started OpenAI's association with Microsoft, and with large numbers of other organizations starting to run AI workloads on Azure's servers, it is on course for huge growth over the next few years.

Story Continues

Azure has been Microsoft's fastest-growing segment for years now; in fiscal Q4, it grew at a 43% clip. That was a slight acceleration from Q3's 40% growth and Q2's 39%. While those are solid growth rates, there is one issue I'm concerned with: Its growth isn't accelerating.

Azure has two primary competitors: Amazon Web Services and Alphabet 's Google Cloud. Both have seen their cloud computing growth rates rapidly accelerate over the same time frame, and I think that is something investors need to grapple with.

Data sources: Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet. Note: Microsoft's fiscal Q4 is equivalent to calendar Q2.

Microsoft's chief competitors in the cloud infrastructure space are seeing rapid cloud growth acceleration, while Azure has only grown marginally. Alphabet also reports next on Oct. 28, while Amazon will deliver results the day after. If Azure continues to grow at a solid 40% or so rate, but Amazon starts to grow at a quicker rate, and Google Cloud reaches a triple-digit growth rate, Microsoft stock could slide in the wake of those reports just because it isn't keeping up with its peers.

These upcoming reports could also have long-term market share ramifications that might make Microsoft look like the least desirable cloud infrastructure stock to own. On the flip side, if Microsoft reports a major acceleration in Azure growth, that could ignite a rally for the stock. We'll see what happens on Oct. 28, but for now, I'm not adding any shares of Microsoft to my portfolio.

news.Title: Is Berkshire Hathaway's Greg Abel Is Changing the Script? Here's the Latest Tech Stock He Just Bought.
news.Content:
That didn't take long. Greg Abel has been CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA)(NYSE: BRKB) since January, and since then he's made several big moves. He bought homebuilder Taylor Morrison in July, although that fits right into the company's standard formula and will be merged with its existing homebuilding operations.

He also presided over a major purchase of Alphabet stock, although the position was initiated by Warren Buffett, who was still the company's chairman at the time.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

His latest move, though, is a further push into tech. Berkshire first bought shares of holding company Bending Spoons (NASDAQ: BSP) in its initial public offering (IPO) in July, and the company just bought an additional $330 million in shares, bringing its total stake to 4% of the company.

Is this where Berkshire Hathaway is heading?

Why Bending Spoons isn't your typical tech stock

CEO Luca Ferrari describes Bending Spoons as "25% private equity, 75% tech company." It's a holding company of sorts, just like Berkshire Hathaway, and it seems to be gaining Abel's admiration.

Instead of acquiring distressed companies and fixing them up before reselling them or taking them public, as many private equity firms do, Bending Spoons acquires great tech companies that need improvement, identifies how to address their problems, helps them perform better, and then keeps them. The Milan-based company's brand portfolio includes Vimeo, Evernote, and AOL, among others, and it recently acquired Airtable.

Similar to Berkshire's recent expansion of its Alphabet holdings, the Bending Spoons position is a private placement, and the company issued 10 million shares to Berkshire at $33 per share. The stock traded at $47 before the announcement, and it jumped to $53 on Oct. 14, when it was announced.

Bending Spoons is a fast-growing tech stock

Abel has said in the past that he's not going to reinvent Berkshire Hathaway . His recent trades are all in line with the company's historical model, and the Bending Spoons position isn't all that different. Although Abel didn't comment on the deal, Bending Spoons' methodology, aside from its tech focus, would appeal to Abel. Berkshire Hathaway loves brand-name companies, although it usually spends its money on companies that have proven their worth, rather than fallen out of favor with their fans.

Story Continues

The company itself is growing fast. In the second quarter, revenue increased 126% to $311 million. However, growth was driven by new acquisitions, and it didn't disclose operating results for its individual brands. Operating income was up 139%, and operating margin improved from 32% to 34%.

Bending Spoons' model is supported by a large credit facility and high debt. It had $793 million in cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter and $1.28 billion in available borrowing capacity, although it has since increased that. Its net debt was $4.09 billion, with a leverage ratio of 2.4. That's not the kind of cash-generating company Berkshire Hathaway usually invests in.

Is this a new direction for Berkshire Hathaway?

The market seemed happy with the news, and Berkshire Hathaway stock has been rising. Its performance year to date has been mediocre, up close to 6%, but it's up 3% over the past week alone.

Bending Spoons itself is based in Italy, but its companies are in the U.S., so it's still a bet on America. Buffett has said that "there remain only a handful of companies in this country capable of truly moving the needle at Berkshire, and they have been endlessly picked over by us and by others." Even under his leadership, the company made investments in Chinese, Japanese, and Latin American companies, and Abel sees opportunities outside the U.S. that could move the needle, too.

Although Berkshire Hathaway seeks to invest in long-term opportunities , it's quick to sell when needed. Some of its recent positions that didn't last very long include Ulta Beauty , Nu Holdings , and Floor & Decor Holdings . Bending Spoons is a riskier company than Berkshire's usual fare, and if it doesn't live up to expectations or Abel feels it's time to move on, it could disappear quickly.

More important for Berkshire Hathaway investors is that Abel appears willing to look beyond the company's traditional industries to move the needle, which bodes well for its future growth.

news.Title: Dear Lam Research Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for October 21
news.Content:
Lam Research (LRCX) is stepping onto the earnings stage after the market closes on Oct. 21, and the mood heading into the report is unlike most. Just weeks ago, Lam Research Chief Financial Officer Doug Bettinger spent two days on two different conference stages. He noted that customers want more tools than the company can ship, and there are no signs of a slowdown.

Now, it's time for analysts and investors to find out how Lam performed for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. Let's take a closer look.

More News from Barchart

Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for October 20

'No Question Tesla's Going to Merge With SpaceX' — Kevin O'Leary Says If You Own Tesla Stock, You'll Own the New Company After Flying Roadster Demo

Charlie Munger Said He Was Still Buying Apartment Complexes 'To Give Me Something To Do' but Ran Them the Opposite Way, 'It's All Deferred Gratification'

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

Why the AI Buildout Runs Through Lam

Lam Research sells etch and deposition equipment used by semiconductor companies to build advanced chips. That puts the company right next to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom as the industry spends on wafer fab equipment (WFE).

CFO Doug Bettinger noted at the Citi Global TMT Conference on Sept. 9 that Lam raised its 2026 WFE estimates from $135 billion to $140 billion, then to the low $150 billion range. Bettinger also said the share of WFE spending Lam can address is now "probably north of 36%," up from the low 30% range and ahead of the pace the company laid out at its last Investor Day.

The reason is chip design. Newer chips, called gate-all-around, are built in 3D. Making them takes more etching, which carves material away, and more deposition, which adds thin layers. Those are the two things where Lam enjoys a competitive moat.

"Gate-all-around is more etch and deposition intensive. It's got selective etch requirements. It's got ALD requirements," Bettinger said. "Those are things we do and things we do really well."

Bettinger said every 100,000 wafer starts of that capacity adds $1 billion to Lam's addressable market. Backside power adds another $1 billion for the same capacity.

A Sold-Out Industry With a Space Problem

At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on Sept. 10, Bettinger was blunt. The industry, he said, is "sold out."

Bettinger noted that Lam's biggest customers, which he calls Tier 1, have eight to 10 new clean rooms coming online between now and the end of 2027. Those customers would not build the clean rooms if they did not plan to equip them.

Story Continues

Lam does not want to be the bottleneck in the supply chain. The company is speeding up its second facility in Malaysia, getting more output from the space it already has, and hiring and training new staff. "Necessity is the mother of invention," Bettinger told the Citi audience on Sept. 9.

Lam Research Vice President of Investor Relations Ram Ganesh added another clue. The company has said that $100 billion of AI data-center spending turns into roughly $8 billion of WFE, but Ganesh believes that figure has since moved $1 billion to $2 billion higher.

In the last quarter, Lam posted a 52% gross margin — its highest in 20 years — and guided 52% for Q1 fiscal 2027. Bettinger said the company now sees a path to the mid-50% range over several years. He credited new products, building closer to customers, and pricing as key reasons for the margin outlook.

Lam's Customer Support Business Group (CSBG) also just posted its third-straight record quarter at nearly $2.5 billion. Bettinger said industry utilization is "basically at 100%," which keeps spare parts moving.

What Does Wall Street Expect on Oct. 21?

So, what do analysts expect Lam Research to post for the September quarter? Based on Yahoo Finance data, analysts estimate revenue of $8.14 billion on average, with a range between roughy $7.9 billion and $8.4 billion. A year ago, revenue came in at $5.32 billion, so that implies year-over-year (YOY) growth of 53% at the midpoint.

In terms of EPS, analysts expect earnings of $2.18 per share for the quarter, up from $1.26 a year ago. Finally, they foresee revenue of $8.54 billion and EPS of $2.32 for the December quarter as well.

For the full year, analysts expect fiscal 2027 revenue of $34.95 billion, up 50% YOY, with EPS of $9.49. For 2028, the revenue forecast stands at $42.11 billion while the EPS estimate is $11.94.

Similarly, using Barchart data, analysts expect EPS of $2.17 for the current quarter, up 72% YOY, and EPS of $9.35 for fiscal 2027, up 61% YOY. For fiscal 2028, EPS is expected to rise 22% YOY to $11.43.

Lam Research beat EPS estimates in each of the last four quarters. Last quarter, the company earned $1.82 against an estimate of $1.69 per share, a beat of roughly 8%.

Why Guidance Matters More Than the Beat

I expect Lam Research to deliver in fiscal Q1. Bettinger's tone and rising estimates both point that way. The bigger question is: What will Lam Research say about the road ahead?

Once earnings are reported, analysts will first want to compare the December outlook provided by management against the $8.54 billion estimate. Then, they should look to gross margin to see whether it holds near 52%. Finally, any update on Lam's Aether dry resist program will be important. Bettinger noted at the Citi conference that he is confident this business will beat its estimated $1.5 billion revenue opportunity, although China growth may prove slower for the company.

Overall, based on 33 analysts with coverage, LRCX stock has a consensus "Strong Buy" rating on Wall Street. Out of those analysts, 23 recommend a "Strong Buy" rating, four have a "Moderate Buy," and six recommend a "Hold" rating. The average price target of $378.30 represents potential upside of 41% from current levels.

news.Content:
儘管近期股市出現波動，知名策略師Tom Lee依然無所畏懼，明確表示自己正「逢低布局 AI 概念股」。

身兼 Fundstrat 研究部門主管的Tom Lee於週一(19日)晚間發給客戶的影音報告中指出：「由於韓國股市跌破 7 月低點，加上市場開始討論 AI 債務疑慮，AI 領域顯然已籠罩在恐慌情緒之中。」

部分投資人將韓股視為參與 AI 行情的替代標的，因此，韓股大盤及 SK海力士( KR000660 ) 等科技權值股下跌，也不時拖累美國半導體與 AI 類股。

Lee 指出，投資人近期面臨「兩個市場、兩種走勢」的局面。根據道瓊市場數據，截至周一收盤，標普 500 等權重指數本月上漲 2.56%，高於市值加權標普 500 指數的 0.51% 漲幅。後者走勢主要由少數大型科技與 AI 企業主導。

標普 500 等權重指數上一次創下歷史新高是在 8 月 13 日，標普 500 指數最近一次創高則是在 10 月 6 日。

Lee 以思科系統( CSCO-US ) 1990 年代的股價表現作為借鏡，解讀這波回檔，並闡述看多美股的理由。

他指出，1993 年至 1994 年網際網路起步時，這檔科技指標股的股價約為 0.8 美元；思科身為路由器供應商，立即成為受惠者。

到了 1997 年初，思科經股票分割調整後的股價已飆升至每股 9 美元，但壓力也逐漸累積。當時，聯準會主席葛林斯潘已提出股市「非理性繁榮」的警告。

隨著市場擔憂貨幣政策緊縮、分析師對思科營收成長轉趨謹慎，以及網際網路協定交換器的競爭疑慮升高，思科股價在當年稍晚跌至 5 美元。

Lee回顧道：「然而一年後，思科從該低點大幅反彈至 18 美元。」雖然 1998 年因俄羅斯國債違約以及長期資本管理公司（LTCM）倒閉引發市場動盪，思科股價再次拉回，但最終到了 2000 年，股價一路攀升至 80 美元，相較於最初的 0.8 美元暴增了 100 倍。

「我覺得我們現在有點像處於這個階段。儘管走勢顛簸，我認為這一切都只是修正，所以我正在逢低買進 AI 股。」
